fragments.label: q001_question
fragments.text: What is the form of government of the United States?

fragments.label: q001_lead_in
fragments.text: You could describe it any of these ways (you only need one):

fragments.label: q001_answer_1
fragments.text: Republic

fragments.label: q001_answer_2
fragments.text: Constitution-based federal republic

fragments.label: q001_answer_3
fragments.text: Representative democracy

fragments.label: q001_disambiguation
fragments.text: We most often hear it called a “representative democracy” — the same idea as a “republic”: we elect people to make the laws for us. That's different from a “direct democracy,” where people vote on every law themselves.

fragments.label: q001_why
fragments.text: In a republic, the power belongs to the people — not a king. We lend it to leaders we elect, and take it back at the next election. In 1787, when kings ruled almost everywhere, trusting regular people to run things was a bold bet.

fragments.label: q001_fun
fragments.text: After the Constitutional Convention, someone asked Benjamin Franklin: did we make a republic or a monarchy? “A republic,” he said, “if you can keep it.” His point: this government was brand-new, and keeping it would take work from every generation.

fragments.label: q002_question
fragments.text: What is the supreme law of the land?

fragments.label: q002_answer_1
fragments.text: (U.S.) Constitution

fragments.label: q002_disambiguation
fragments.text: Don't mix these up: the “supreme law of the land” is the Constitution itself — not the “Supreme Court.” One is the rulebook; the other is the referee.

fragments.label: q002_why
fragments.text: Even the President has to obey the Constitution. That's the big idea: no one in America is above the law — not even the most powerful person. The law itself is the boss.

fragments.label: q002_fun
fragments.text: Long ago, Maryland tried to tax a national bank to death. The Supreme Court said no — one state can't destroy what the whole country builds. That's how we learned: when state and national law collide, national law wins.

fragments.label: q003_question
fragments.text: Name one thing the U.S. Constitution does.

fragments.label: q003_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to name one — the Constitution does all of these:

fragments.label: q003_answer_1
fragments.text: Forms the government

fragments.label: q003_answer_2
fragments.text: Defines powers of government

fragments.label: q003_answer_3
fragments.text: Defines the parts of government

fragments.label: q003_answer_4
fragments.text: Protects the rights of the people

fragments.label: q003_why
fragments.text: In 1787, most countries ran on a king's word or unwritten custom. The Constitution did something new — it wrote the rules down. It builds the government (a Congress to make laws, a President to enforce them, courts to judge) and limits it too, by protecting people's rights.

fragments.label: q003_fun
fragments.text: Of every written national constitution on Earth, the U.S. Constitution is both the oldest still in use and one of the shortest — only about 4,500 words. The whole rulebook for the government is shorter than many a school essay.

fragments.label: q004_question
fragments.text: The U.S. Constitution starts with the words “We the People.” What does “We the People” mean?

fragments.label: q004_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need one — these all point at the same big idea:

fragments.label: q004_answer_1
fragments.text: Self-government

fragments.label: q004_answer_2
fragments.text: Popular sovereignty

fragments.label: q004_answer_3
fragments.text: Consent of the governed

fragments.label: q004_answer_4
fragments.text: People should govern themselves

fragments.label: q004_answer_5
fragments.text: (Example of) social contract

fragments.label: q004_disambiguation
fragments.text: All of these mean the same thing in different words: the people are in charge of the government, not the other way around.

fragments.label: q004_why
fragments.text: These words flipped history. For ages, kings held the power and the people obeyed. “We the People” says the opposite: the government's power comes from regular people — and belongs to them.

fragments.label: q004_fun
fragments.text: An early draft of the Constitution started by naming all thirteen states, one by one. A delegate changed it to just three words: “We the People.” That small change meant the country belonged to its people — not to thirteen separate states.

fragments.label: q005_question
fragments.text: How are changes made to the U.S. Constitution?

fragments.label: q005_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q005_answer_1
fragments.text: Amendments

fragments.label: q005_answer_2
fragments.text: The amendment process

fragments.label: q005_why
fragments.text: The Founders knew they wouldn't get everything right. So they built in a way to fix the Constitution — by adding amendments — but made it hard, so it changes only when almost the whole country agrees.

fragments.label: q005_fun
fragments.text: People have tried to change the Constitution more than 11,000 times. Only 27 of those changes ever made it in. It's that hard on purpose — so the rules change only when nearly everyone agrees.

fragments.label: q006_question
fragments.text: What does the Bill of Rights protect?

fragments.label: q006_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q006_answer_1
fragments.text: (The basic) rights of Americans

fragments.label: q006_answer_2
fragments.text: (The basic) rights of people living in the United States

fragments.label: q006_disambiguation
fragments.text: Notice: it protects the rights of everyone living in the United States — not only citizens.

fragments.label: q006_why
fragments.text: The Bill of Rights flips the usual question. Instead of listing what people may do, it lists what the government may NOT do to them — like silence your speech or your religion. These are freedoms no leader can take away.

fragments.label: q006_fun
fragments.text: Our famous First Amendment — free speech and religion — was almost the Third! Twelve changes were proposed; the first two didn't pass back then, so number three jumped to the top. Even our rights were chosen one by one.

fragments.label: q006_mnemonic
fragments.text: Count the Bill of Rights on your hands: ten amendments, ten fingers.

fragments.label: q007_question
fragments.text: How many amendments does the U.S. Constitution have?

fragments.label: q007_answer_1
fragments.text: Twenty-seven (27)

fragments.label: q007_why
fragments.text: The Constitution is hard to change on purpose. In over 230 years, Americans have agreed to update it just 27 times. Hard enough to protect the rules; possible enough to fix them when something really must change.

fragments.label: q007_fun
fragments.text: In 1982, a UT Austin sophomore named Gregory Watson wrote a paper arguing a forgotten amendment from 1789 could still be ratified. His professor gave him a C. He spent the next ten years pushing states to vote on it — and that C-grade paper became the 27th Amendment.

fragments.label: q008_question
fragments.text: Why is the Declaration of Independence important?

fragments.label: q008_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to give one reason. Any of these works:

fragments.label: q008_answer_1
fragments.text: It says America is free from British control.

fragments.label: q008_answer_2
fragments.text: It says all people are created equal.

fragments.label: q008_answer_3
fragments.text: It identifies inherent rights.

fragments.label: q008_answer_4
fragments.text: It identifies individual freedoms.

fragments.label: q008_why
fragments.text: The Declaration didn't just declare independence — it told the world why. 'All people are created equal' with rights no government can take away. Those words would be quoted back by every American fight for justice that came after: abolition, suffrage, civil rights.

fragments.label: q008_fun
fragments.text: John Adams was sure Americans would celebrate Independence Day forever — 'with pomp and parade,' he wrote his wife. He was right about the party. He was wrong about the date. Adams meant July 2nd, the day Congress voted to break with Britain. We celebrate July 4th instead.

fragments.label: q009_question
fragments.text: What founding document said the American colonies were free from Britain?

fragments.label: q009_answer_1
fragments.text: Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q009_disambiguation
fragments.text: Easy to mix up with the Constitution. Different jobs: the Declaration of Independence (1776) said we're leaving. The Constitution (1787) said here's how the new country works. One is the goodbye letter; the other is the rulebook.

fragments.label: q009_why
fragments.text: This was the public, official break — written down for everyone to read. Before it, the colonies were complaining. After it, they were a new country — though the war would last seven more years to make that true on the ground.

fragments.label: q009_fun
fragments.text: Did you know the original Declaration went into hiding for 6 years during the war with England moving from location to location in secret?

fragments.label: q010_question
fragments.text: Name two important ideas from the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.

fragments.label: q010_lead_in
fragments.text: Six big ideas appear in both documents — name any two:

fragments.label: q010_answer_1
fragments.text: Equality

fragments.label: q010_answer_2
fragments.text: Liberty

fragments.label: q010_answer_3
fragments.text: Social contract

fragments.label: q010_answer_4
fragments.text: Natural rights

fragments.label: q010_answer_5
fragments.text: Limited government

fragments.label: q010_answer_6
fragments.text: Self-government

fragments.label: q010_why
fragments.text: These ideas weren't normal at the time. Most countries were ruled by kings who claimed God put them in charge. The American documents said the opposite: power comes from people, government is limited, and rights belong to everyone. That was the radical bet.

fragments.label: q010_fun
fragments.text: When colonists said power comes from 'the consent of the governed,' they flipped centuries of European thinking upside down. Most kings claimed God put them in charge. Americans said: actually, you only get to lead if we let you. That single idea changed how the world thinks about government.

fragments.label: q011_question
fragments.text: The words "Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness" are in what founding document?

fragments.label: q011_answer_1
fragments.text: Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q011_why
fragments.text: These words say what American government is for: protecting your right to live, to be free, and to chase what makes you flourish — not just to obey rulers. Most governments at the time existed to serve the king. America said: the state exists to serve YOU.

fragments.label: q011_fun
fragments.text: Jefferson borrowed these three famous ideas from English philosopher John Locke, who originally wrote: 'life, liberty, and property.' Jefferson swapped 'property' for 'pursuit of happiness' — a much bigger promise. Government's job wasn't just to protect what you own, but to help you flourish.

fragments.label: q012_question
fragments.text: What is the economic system of the United States?

fragments.label: q012_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q012_answer_1
fragments.text: Capitalism

fragments.label: q012_answer_2
fragments.text: Free market economy

fragments.label: q012_why
fragments.text: In a free market economy, people decide what to make, buy, and sell — not the government. You can start a business, own property, and keep what you earn. That freedom is what let American companies — from corner stores to Apple — get invented by ordinary people.

fragments.label: q012_fun
fragments.text: The U.S. Constitution never uses the words 'capitalism' or 'free market' — those terms came later. But Article I, Section 8 set the foundation: it gave inventors and writers exclusive rights to their own creations. That made the U.S. the first country to put inventor rights into its national constitution.

fragments.label: q013_question
fragments.text: What is the rule of law?

fragments.label: q013_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to give one. Any of these works:

fragments.label: q013_answer_1
fragments.text: Everyone must follow the law.

fragments.label: q013_answer_2
fragments.text: Leaders must obey the law.

fragments.label: q013_answer_3
fragments.text: Government must obey the law.

fragments.label: q013_answer_4
fragments.text: No one is above the law.

fragments.label: q013_why
fragments.text: Rule of law means the laws apply to everyone — including the most powerful. The president must follow the same rules as a school teacher. A senator can be sued. Without this idea, leaders do whatever they want. With it, no one can use their power to hurt people unfairly.

fragments.label: q013_fun
fragments.text: John Adams wrote one of the most famous phrases in American law — 'a government of laws, and not of men.' But he didn't write it for the U.S. Constitution. He wrote it for the Massachusetts state constitution, which he drafted years before the federal Constitution even existed. Leaders still quote his line today.

fragments.label: q014_question
fragments.text: Many documents influenced the U.S. Constitution. Name one.

fragments.label: q014_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to name one. Any of these works:

fragments.label: q014_answer_1
fragments.text: Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q014_answer_2
fragments.text: Articles of Confederation

fragments.label: q014_answer_3
fragments.text: Federalist Papers

fragments.label: q014_answer_4
fragments.text: Iroquois Great Law of Peace

fragments.label: q014_why
fragments.text: The Constitution didn't appear from nowhere. The founders read history, philosophy, and other documents — argued for years — then borrowed the best ideas. Knowing what shaped it shows that the Constitution is a careful mix of older ideas, not one person's invention.

fragments.label: q014_fun
fragments.text: In 1988, the U.S. Congress passed Resolution 331 officially acknowledging that the Iroquois Confederacy's system of government influenced America's founders. The Iroquois had already united six native nations under shared rules long before the U.S. Constitution was written. Benjamin Franklin studied their system closely.

fragments.label: q015_question
fragments.text: There are three branches of government. Why?

fragments.label: q015_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to give one reason:

fragments.label: q015_answer_1
fragments.text: So one part does not become too powerful

fragments.label: q015_answer_2
fragments.text: Checks and balances

fragments.label: q015_answer_3
fragments.text: Separation of powers

fragments.label: q015_why
fragments.text: Splitting power into three branches means no one branch can grab too much. Each can check the others — the president can veto laws, the courts can strike them down, Congress can override the president. That tug-of-war was designed on purpose. Slow and messy, but it prevents tyranny.

fragments.label: q015_fun
fragments.text: James Madison explained why we need three separate branches in one perfect line in Federalist Paper No. 51 (1788): 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.' His point: people aren't perfect, so power needs to check power. Split government in three, and no single piece can get too strong.

fragments.label: q016_question
fragments.text: Name the three branches of government.

fragments.label: q016_lead_in
fragments.text: Name all three:

fragments.label: q016_answer_1
fragments.text: Legislative (Congress)

fragments.label: q016_answer_2
fragments.text: Executive (president)

fragments.label: q016_answer_3
fragments.text: Judicial (the courts)

fragments.label: q016_why
fragments.text: Knowing the three branches helps you understand who does what in your government. Congress writes the laws. The president carries them out. The courts decide what the laws mean and whether they're constitutional. Three different jobs, three different sets of people in charge.

fragments.label: q016_fun
fragments.text: Article III of the Constitution — which creates the entire judicial branch — is famously brief. It barely says anything about how the Supreme Court should actually work day-to-day. Nearly every detail about how the Court operates was figured out over the next 230 years, often by the Court itself.

fragments.label: q017_question
fragments.text: The President of the United States is in charge of which branch of government?

fragments.label: q017_answer_1
fragments.text: Executive branch

fragments.label: q017_why
fragments.text: The president runs the executive branch — the part that carries out laws Congress passes. The president also commands the military, signs treaties, and picks Supreme Court nominees. Powerful job, but limited: the president can't make laws, can't ignore court rulings, and can be removed by Congress.

fragments.label: q017_fun
fragments.text: When George Washington took office in 1789, nobody knew what to call him. Vice President John Adams pushed for 'His Highness, the President of the United States, and Protector of their Liberties.' The Senate agreed. The House refused. After weeks of debate, they settled on plain 'Mr. President.'

fragments.label: q018_question
fragments.text: What part of the federal government writes laws?

fragments.label: q018_lead_in
fragments.text: Any of these answers works:

fragments.label: q018_answer_1
fragments.text: (U.S.) Congress

fragments.label: q018_answer_2
fragments.text: The legislative branch

fragments.label: q018_why
fragments.text: Only Congress can write new federal laws — not the president, not the courts . That's a deliberate choice. The people who make laws should be the ones the public elects and can vote out. If you don't like a law, you can fire the people who wrote it next election.

fragments.label: q018_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution describes Congress in Article I — the longest article by far. The founders put Congress first and gave it the most space because they expected Congress to be the most powerful (and most dangerous) branch. Notice the order: Article I is the lawmakers; the president comes second.

fragments.label: q019_question
fragments.text: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?

fragments.label: q019_lead_in
fragments.text: Name both:

fragments.label: q019_answer_1
fragments.text: The Senate

fragments.label: q019_answer_2
fragments.text: The House of Representatives

fragments.label: q019_why
fragments.text: The two parts of Congress check each other. A bill must pass both the House (where seats depend on state population) and the Senate (where every state gets equal power) before it can become law. Bigger states can't bully smaller ones; smaller states can't block everything.

fragments.label: q019_fun
fragments.text: The Constitutional Convention almost broke apart in summer 1787 over a single question: should states get equal votes, or should bigger states get more? The Connecticut Compromise saved it — every state gets two senators (equal), but House seats depend on population. The deal passed by a single vote.

fragments.label: q020_question
fragments.text: Name one power of the U.S. Congress.

fragments.label: q020_lead_in
fragments.text: You only need to name one. Any of these works:

fragments.label: q020_answer_1
fragments.text: Writes laws

fragments.label: q020_answer_2
fragments.text: Declares war

fragments.label: q020_answer_3
fragments.text: Makes the federal budget

fragments.label: q020_why
fragments.text: Congress holds the most powerful tools in government: the power to write laws, declare war, and decide how every federal dollar gets spent. No president can declare war, spend money, or pass a law without Congress. That's why the founders made Congress first — and biggest — in the Constitution.

fragments.label: q020_fun
fragments.text: Congress hasn't formally declared war since 1942. Every U.S. conflict since — Korea, Vietnam, the Gulf War, Iraq, Afghanistan — used a different tool: 'authorization for use of military force.' Same effect, different name.

fragments.label: q021_question
fragments.text: How many U.S. senators are there?

fragments.label: q021_answer_1
fragments.text: One hundred (100)

fragments.label: q021_why
fragments.text: Two senators per state, times 50 states, equals 100. Equal representation means Wyoming (584,000 people) and California (39 million people) each get exactly two votes in the Senate. That's intentional — it forces leaders to listen to small states too, not just the big ones.

fragments.label: q021_fun
fragments.text: The Vice President of the United States acts as the President of the Senate, but is only permitted to vote to break a legislative tie

fragments.label: q022_question
fragments.text: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?

fragments.label: q022_answer_1
fragments.text: Six (6) years

fragments.label: q022_why
fragments.text: Six-year terms let senators think long-term — passing laws that take years to pay off, casting unpopular but right votes without immediately facing voters. Compare that to House members (2 years), who must constantly campaign. Different terms, different temperaments — by design.

fragments.label: q022_fun
fragments.text: On May 15, 1789, the first U.S. Senate literally drew lots from a box to decide how long they served. Some senators drew Class 1 (2 years), others Class 2 (4 years), others Class 3 (6 years). That random drawing set up the staggered elections still used today.

fragments.label: q023_question
fragments.text: Who is one of your state's U.S. senators now?

fragments.label: q023_answer_1
fragments.text: Answers will vary by state. (D.C. and U.S. territories have no senators.)

fragments.label: q023_disambiguation
fragments.text: District of Columbia residents and U.S. territory residents should answer that D.C. (or the territory) has no U.S. senators.

fragments.label: q023_why
fragments.text: Your two senators represent your entire state in Washington. They write laws, vote on Supreme Court nominees, approve treaties, and decide federal spending. Knowing their names — and being able to contact them — is how regular citizens influence federal decisions.

fragments.label: q023_fun
fragments.text: Whoever your senators are right now, they sit at one of 100 desks in the Senate chamber that have been used for over 200 years. For more than 120 years, senators have inscribed their names inside the desk drawer when they leave. Daniel Webster's old desk is still used today by senators from New Hampshire.

fragments.label: q024_question
fragments.text: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?

fragments.label: q024_answer_1
fragments.text: Four hundred thirty-five (435)

fragments.label: q024_why
fragments.text: The House has 435 members so representation roughly matches population. California gets 52 representatives; Wyoming only gets 1. More people means more voices in the House — unlike the Senate, where Wyoming and California each get exactly 2 senators.

fragments.label: q024_fun
fragments.text: The number of representatives in the House grew with the country until 1929. The first House had 65 members in 1789, then expanded after each census — 105, 142, 213, all the way to 435 by 1913. Then Congress passed the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, capping the House at 435 forever — even as the U.S. population kept growing.

fragments.label: q025_question
fragments.text: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?

fragments.label: q025_answer_1
fragments.text: Two (2) years

fragments.label: q025_why
fragments.text: Every two years, the entire House faces reelection. That's the shortest term in federal government. If you don't like what your representative is doing, you don't have to wait long to vote them out. It's designed to keep representatives close to the people.

fragments.label: q025_fun
fragments.text: In 1788, James Madison argued for two-year House terms in Federalist 52. He wrote that the House 'should have an immediate dependence on, and an intimate sympathy with the people.' Two-year terms force representatives to listen to voters constantly.

fragments.label: q026_question
fragments.text: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?

fragments.label: q026_answer_1
fragments.text: To more closely follow public opinion

fragments.label: q026_why
fragments.text: House members with 2-year terms feel public opinion fast. They vote on what people care about right now. The Senate, with 6-year terms, can take a longer view — including making unpopular calls when needed. The two chambers were designed to balance each other.

fragments.label: q026_fun
fragments.text: There's a famous old story: When Jefferson returned from France in 1789, he asked Washington why the Convention created a Senate. Washington pointed to Jefferson's saucer of cooling tea: 'We pour legislation into the senatorial saucer to cool it.'

fragments.label: q026_mnemonic
fragments.text: House = hot tea (passionate, fast, 2-year terms); Senate = saucer that cools it (deliberative, slow, 6-year terms).

fragments.label: q027_question
fragments.text: How many senators does each state have?

fragments.label: q027_answer_1
fragments.text: Two (2)

fragments.label: q027_why
fragments.text: Two senators is the magic number. One could die or be sick, leaving a state unrepresented. Three or more would have made the Senate huge and unwieldy. Two means each state always has someone in the chamber — and an equal voice with every other state.

fragments.label: q027_fun
fragments.text: Two senators per state is one of the only things in the Constitution that can never be changed by amendment. Article V says no state can be 'deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate' without its own consent. Translation: Wyoming will have exactly two senators forever, no matter how big or small it grows.

fragments.label: q028_question
fragments.text: Why does each state have two senators?

fragments.label: q028_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q028_answer_1
fragments.text: Equal representation (for small states)

fragments.label: q028_answer_2
fragments.text: The Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise)

fragments.label: q028_why
fragments.text: If senators were assigned by population, big states would dominate the Senate the same way they dominate the House. Small states feared that. The compromise — equal Senate representation — was the only way to keep small states in the Union. Without it, there might be no United States.

fragments.label: q028_fun
fragments.text: James Madison — the 'Father of the Constitution' — actually opposed giving each state two senators. He wanted representation in both chambers based on population, so big states would have more votes. Madison lost the fight. The small states won. That compromise still shapes who has power in Washington today.

fragments.label: q029_question
fragments.text: Name your U.S. representative.

fragments.label: q029_answer_1
fragments.text: Answers will vary by congressional district.

fragments.label: q029_disambiguation
fragments.text: Residents of U.S. territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may name that Delegate or Commissioner. It's also acceptable to state that the territory has no voting representatives in Congress.

fragments.label: q029_why
fragments.text: Your representative is your closest voice in the federal government. They represent your specific district — usually a smaller area than your senators cover. You're more likely to meet them at a town hall or get their staff's help with a federal problem. Knowing who they are matters.

fragments.label: q029_fun
fragments.text: In 1790, each House member represented about 30,000 people. Today, the average representative speaks for over 700,000 people — about 25 times more. The House is the same size (435), but the country has grown enormously. So your representative carries 25 times the weight of one in 1789.

fragments.label: q030_question
fragments.text: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?

fragments.label: q030_answer_1
fragments.text: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives.

fragments.label: q030_why
fragments.text: The Speaker is the leader of the House of Representatives — chosen by the House itself. The Speaker decides which bills come up for a vote, runs floor debate, and is second in line to the presidency after the Vice President. It's one of the most powerful jobs in American government.

fragments.label: q030_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution doesn't actually require the Speaker to be a member of the House. In theory, any U.S. citizen could be elected Speaker — though every one of the 56 Speakers since 1789 has been a sitting Representative. The Speaker is also second in line to the presidency, right after the Vice President.

fragments.label: q031_question
fragments.text: Who does a U.S. senator represent?

fragments.label: q031_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q031_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens of their state

fragments.label: q031_answer_2
fragments.text: People of their state

fragments.label: q031_why
fragments.text: Each senator represents every person in their state — the people who voted for them and the people who didn't. They're not assigned a small district like House members. Senators have to listen to ranchers, teachers, immigrants, business owners, and millions of others — all in their one state.

fragments.label: q031_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution requires senators to actually live in the state they represent — they can't represent California while living in Texas. The framers picked the word 'inhabitant' on purpose, to make sure senators were rooted in their states and knew their state's needs first-hand.

fragments.label: q032_question
fragments.text: Who elects U.S. senators?

fragments.label: q032_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens from their state

fragments.label: q032_why
fragments.text: Senators serve six years, so each one represents your state's voice in Washington for a long time. Because voters elect them directly, senators have to answer to ordinary citizens.

fragments.label: q032_fun
fragments.text: For 124 years, you couldn't vote for your senator. State legislatures chose them, as the Constitution originally required. Senate seats sometimes sat empty for months when state legislatures deadlocked over who to pick. The 17th Amendment (1913) finally let voters elect senators directly, a huge shift in American democracy.

fragments.label: q033_question
fragments.text: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?

fragments.label: q033_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens in their (congressional) district

fragments.label: q033_answer_2
fragments.text: People in their (congressional) district

fragments.label: q033_why
fragments.text: Your representative speaks only for your specific district — usually a smaller area than what your senators cover. That's why they're often called the closest federal officials to ordinary people. They handle constituent concerns, hold town halls in your area, and write laws shaped by your community's needs.

fragments.label: q033_fun
fragments.text: The word 'gerrymander', is a negative term for redrawing voting maps in a way to get more votes. In 1812, A Boston cartoonist drew an oddly-shaped Massachusetts voting district as a winged salamander. Governor Elbridge Gerry had signed it into law — so 'Gerry' + 'salamander' = 'gerrymander.'

fragments.label: q034_question
fragments.text: Who elects members of the House of Representatives?

fragments.label: q034_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens from their (congressional) district

fragments.label: q034_why
fragments.text: Voters in your district — and only your district — choose your representative.

fragments.label: q034_fun
fragments.text: John Quincy Adams remains the only President elected to the U.S. House of Representatives after his service as commander in chief

fragments.label: q035_question
fragments.text: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?

fragments.label: q035_answer_1
fragments.text: (Because of) the state's population

fragments.label: q035_answer_2
fragments.text: (Because) they have more people

fragments.label: q035_answer_3
fragments.text: (Because) some states have more people

fragments.label: q035_why
fragments.text: Larger states get more Congressional representatives because more people live there. This is the 'proportional' part of representation, it is balanced by the Senate, where every state has 2 senators regardless of size.

fragments.label: q035_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution promises every state at least 1 representative — no matter how small. So Wyoming, with 580,000 people, gets 1. California, with 39 million, gets 52.

fragments.label: q036_question
fragments.text: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?

fragments.label: q036_answer_1
fragments.text: Four (4) years

fragments.label: q036_why
fragments.text: Four years gives a president enough time to actually accomplish something — but not so long that voters lose their power to change course. The Founders specifically designed it to balance effectiveness with accountability.

fragments.label: q036_fun
fragments.text: The Founders argued for months over how long the president should serve. Proposals ranged from 3 to 15 years — and even 'during Good Behavior' (a polite way to say for life). One delegate sarcastically proposed 20 years, 'the medium life of princes.' In late August 1787, they finally settled on 4.

fragments.label: q037_question
fragments.text: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?

fragments.label: q037_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q037_answer_1
fragments.text: (Because of) the 22nd Amendment

fragments.label: q037_answer_2
fragments.text: To keep the president from becoming too powerful

fragments.label: q037_why
fragments.text: Two terms is enough time for a president to govern, but not so long that they become a permanent ruler. The limit is a deliberate guardrail against the kind of one-person power the colonists rebelled against. It keeps the presidency — even with all its power — temporary, accountable, and democratic.

fragments.label: q037_fun
fragments.text: George Washington could have ruled for life — but chose to step down after 8 years. His example held for 144 years. Then Franklin D. Roosevelt broke it, winning 4 terms during the Depression and WWII. After he died in office, Congress proposed the 22nd Amendment to lock in the two-term limit. Ratified 1951.

fragments.label: q038_question
fragments.text: What is the name of the President of the United States now?

fragments.label: q038_answer_1
fragments.text: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the President of the United States.

fragments.label: q038_why
fragments.text: The President is the head of the executive branch and Commander in Chief of the military. They sign or veto bills, appoint federal judges, and lead American foreign policy.

fragments.label: q038_fun
fragments.text: The presidential oath is only 35 words: starting with 'I do solemnly swear that I will faithfully execute the Office of President...'

fragments.label: q039_question
fragments.text: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?

fragments.label: q039_answer_1
fragments.text: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.

fragments.label: q039_why
fragments.text: The Vice President is first in line to become President if the President can no longer serve. The VP also presides over the Senate and breaks tied votes — a job that has decided huge laws over the years. It's a unique role: half executive branch, half legislative branch.

fragments.label: q039_fun
fragments.text: The Vice President's only constitutional jobs are to preside over the Senate and break tied votes. John Adams, the first VP, called it 'the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived.' But the VP is first in line if the President can't serve — so the 'insignificant' job is just a heartbeat from the most powerful one.

fragments.label: q040_question
fragments.text: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?

fragments.label: q040_answer_1
fragments.text: The Vice President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q040_why
fragments.text: America has had eight presidents die in office and one resign — and every single time, the Vice President took over smoothly. The succession plan is what makes American democracy stable through crisis.

fragments.label: q040_fun
fragments.text: In 1841, President William Henry Harrison died after just 32 days in office. Did the VP become the full president, or just 'acting president'? Nobody knew. Vice President John Tyler took the oath and insisted he was now the full president. The Constitution didn't formally confirm this until the 25th Amendment in 1967.

fragments.label: q041_question
fragments.text: Name one power of the president.

fragments.label: q041_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q041_answer_1
fragments.text: Signs bills into law

fragments.label: q041_answer_2
fragments.text: Vetoes bills

fragments.label: q041_answer_3
fragments.text: Enforces laws

fragments.label: q041_answer_4
fragments.text: Commander in Chief (of the military)

fragments.label: q041_answer_5
fragments.text: Chief diplomat

fragments.label: q041_answer_6
fragments.text: Appoints federal judges

fragments.label: q041_why
fragments.text: The president wears many hats: signing laws, vetoing bills, leading the military, negotiating treaties, appointing judges. Each role gives the president huge influence — but each one is also balanced by Congress or the courts. That's the system the Founders built so no single person could rule alone.

fragments.label: q041_fun
fragments.text: Of all the President's powers, only one has almost no check: to pardon guilty people. Congress can override a veto. The Senate must approve treaties and judges. Courts can rule actions unconstitutional. But the Supreme Court has called the pardon power 'unlimited except in cases of impeachment.'

fragments.label: q042_question
fragments.text: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?

fragments.label: q042_answer_1
fragments.text: The President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q042_why
fragments.text: Putting the President — a civilian — in charge of the military is one of the most important rules in American government. It means the people elect the person who commands the army, not a general. The military follows orders from the elected leader. That's how America avoids the danger of military rule.

fragments.label: q042_fun
fragments.text: In 1783, after winning the Revolutionary War, General Washington could have ruled as king. Instead, he resigned his military commission to Congress, handing power back to civilians. King George III reportedly called him 'the greatest man in the world.' That set the rule we still follow: civilians, not generals, command the U.S. military.

fragments.label: q043_question
fragments.text: Who signs bills to become laws?

fragments.label: q043_answer_1
fragments.text: The President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q043_why
fragments.text: After Congress passes a bill, it isn't law yet — the President has to sign it. That signature is the final step that turns the idea Congress agreed on into a rule everyone in America has to follow.

fragments.label: q043_fun
fragments.text: Signing a major bill is often a ceremony. President Lyndon Johnson used more than 75 pens to sign the Civil Rights Act of 1964 — and gave every pen away as a gift. One of the first went to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

fragments.label: q044_question
fragments.text: Who vetoes bills?

fragments.label: q044_answer_1
fragments.text: The President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q044_why
fragments.text: The veto is the President's biggest tool to push back on Congress. When the President disagrees with a bill, a veto can stop it from becoming law. But the system has a check on the check: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

fragments.label: q044_fun
fragments.text: Presidents use the veto very differently. Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed 635 bills — the all-time record. George Washington vetoed just 2 in his entire 8 years. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers, but it's so hard that only about 4% of all vetoes have ever been overturned.

fragments.label: q045_question
fragments.text: Who appoints federal judges?

fragments.label: q045_answer_1
fragments.text: The President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q045_why
fragments.text: The President picks federal judges — including Supreme Court Justices — but the Senate must confirm them. That partnership is one of the Constitution's clearest checks. And because federal judges serve for life, the President's choices can shape American law long after the President's own term ends.

fragments.label: q045_fun
fragments.text: Federal judges aren't elected — they're picked by the President, confirmed by the Senate, and then serve for life (unless they resign or are impeached). So a president's judicial picks can outlast their own term by decades. Justice Clarence Thomas, appointed in 1991, has served 35 years and counting.

fragments.label: q046_question
fragments.text: The executive branch has many parts. Name one.

fragments.label: q046_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q046_answer_1
fragments.text: President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q046_answer_2
fragments.text: The President's Cabinet

fragments.label: q046_answer_3
fragments.text: Federal departments and agencies

fragments.label: q046_why
fragments.text: The executive branch is much bigger than just the President. The President leads it, but it includes the Cabinet, top advisers running the major departments, plus federal agencies like the FBI, NASA, and the Department of Education. Millions of federal workers carry out the laws Congress passes every single day.

fragments.label: q046_fun
fragments.text: In 1789, Washington's first Cabinet had just four advisers: Jefferson at State, Hamilton at Treasury, Knox at War, and Randolph as Attorney General. Today there are 15 Cabinet departments. The newest was added in 2002: Homeland Security, created in response to the September 11th attacks.

fragments.label: q047_question
fragments.text: What does the President's Cabinet do?

fragments.label: q047_answer_1
fragments.text: Advises the President (of the United States)

fragments.label: q047_why
fragments.text: The Cabinet brings experts together to advise the President on the country's biggest issues. Each member runs a major department, so they know their area in depth. When the President faces a hard choice — go to war, fix the economy, respond to a disaster — the Cabinet is where the conversation usually happens.

fragments.label: q047_fun
fragments.text: The Cabinet isn't actually in the Constitution! The Convention debated adding a 'Council of State' to advise the President but rejected it. Article II only lets the President ask for 'Opinions in writing' from department heads. Washington found that too slow and started holding in-person meetings in 1791 — inventing the Cabinet we know today.

fragments.label: q048_question
fragments.text: What are two Cabinet-level positions?

fragments.label: q048_lead_in
fragments.text: Name any two of these:

fragments.label: q048_answer_1
fragments.text: The Attorney General

fragments.label: q048_answer_2
fragments.text: Secretary of Commerce

fragments.label: q048_answer_3
fragments.text: Secretary of Education

fragments.label: q048_answer_4
fragments.text: Secretary of Energy

fragments.label: q048_answer_5
fragments.text: Secretary of State

fragments.label: q048_answer_6
fragments.text: Secretary of War (Defense)

fragments.label: q048_why
fragments.text: Cabinet-level positions are the senior leaders who run the federal government's biggest departments and agencies — from defense and diplomacy to schools and intelligence. Knowing some of them shows you understand how the executive branch actually operates day-to-day, beyond just the President.

fragments.label: q048_fun
fragments.text: Most Cabinet heads are called 'Secretary' — but one isn't. Why is the head of the Justice Department called 'Attorney General'? Because for 81 years there was no Department of Justice! The Attorney General was created in 1789, and Congress didn't create the Justice Department until 1870.

fragments.label: q049_question
fragments.text: Why is the Electoral College important?

fragments.label: q049_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q049_answer_1
fragments.text: It decides who is elected president.

fragments.label: q049_answer_2
fragments.text: The electoral college provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.

fragments.label: q049_why
fragments.text: The Electoral College is how America actually picks its president. Each state gets electors based on its size in Congress — total 538 nationwide. The system was a compromise: it kept Congress from choosing the president outright, but also avoided a pure national vote the framers feared. It's still how we elect presidents today.

fragments.label: q049_fun
fragments.text: In 1800, the original Electoral College broke. Jefferson and Burr — running mates from the same party! — tied with 73 electoral votes each. The House deadlocked through 35 ballots over five days. On the 36th time voting, Hamilton broke the stalemate by backing Jefferson. The 12th Amendment (1804) fixed the system so a tie like that couldn't happen again.

fragments.label: q050_question
fragments.text: What is one part of the judicial branch?

fragments.label: q050_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q050_answer_1
fragments.text: Supreme Court

fragments.label: q050_answer_2
fragments.text: Federal Courts

fragments.label: q050_why
fragments.text: 'Judicial' means relating to courts or judges. The judicial branch is the system of courts that interprets the law. At the top is the Supreme Court — the final word on every federal legal question. Below it are the federal district courts and courts of appeals.

fragments.label: q050_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution requires only one court — the Supreme Court. Article III says 'one supreme Court, and such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.' Every other federal court — district courts, courts of appeals — exists only because Congress chose to create them, starting with the Judiciary Act of 1789.

fragments.label: q051_question
fragments.text: What does the judicial branch do?

fragments.label: q051_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q051_answer_1
fragments.text: Reviews laws

fragments.label: q051_answer_2
fragments.text: Explains laws

fragments.label: q051_answer_3
fragments.text: Resolves disputes (disagreements) about the law

fragments.label: q051_answer_4
fragments.text: Decides if a law goes against the (U.S.) Constitution

fragments.label: q051_why
fragments.text: Courts settle arguments — between people, between businesses, between citizens and the government. They also do something deeper: they check whether laws follow the Constitution. If a law violates the Constitution, courts can strike it down.

fragments.label: q051_fun
fragments.text: The judicial branch's greatest power isn't actually stated in the Constitution! Chief Justice John Marshall claimed it for the Supreme Court in the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison. He wrote that it is 'the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' That power — declaring a law unconstitutional — has shaped American law ever since.

fragments.label: q052_question
fragments.text: What is the highest court in the United States?

fragments.label: q052_answer_1
fragments.text: The Supreme Court

fragments.label: q052_why
fragments.text: The Supreme Court is the final word on every federal legal question. No higher court can overrule it. When the Justices decide what the Constitution means, that meaning becomes the law for the whole country.

fragments.label: q052_fun
fragments.text: The Supreme Court first met on February 1, 1790, in a New York City market building called the Royal Exchange. But only 3 of the 6 justices showed up! When enough judges were present up to make a 'quorum,' meaning a large enough percentage to vote, they didn't have any cases to decide yet.

fragments.label: q053_question
fragments.text: How many seats are on the Supreme Court?

fragments.label: q053_answer_1
fragments.text: Nine (9)

fragments.label: q053_why
fragments.text: Nine justices share the work of the highest court — one Chief Justice and eight Associate Justices. Together they hear cases, debate the meaning of the law, and vote. An odd number means there's almost always a clear majority.

fragments.label: q053_fun
fragments.text: The Constitution doesn't set the size of the Supreme Court — Congress does! The Court has had 6, 7, 9, and even 10 justices over its history. It's been 9 since 1869. In 1937, President Franklin D. Roosevelt tried to expand it to 15 to win the rulings he wanted. Congress refused, and the number has stayed at 9 ever since.

fragments.label: q054_question
fragments.text: How many Supreme Court justices are usually needed to decide a case?

fragments.label: q054_answer_1
fragments.text: Five (5)

fragments.label: q054_why
fragments.text: Five out of nine is a simple majority — the smallest number of justices who can make a ruling stick. That's why so many of the biggest Supreme Court decisions are 5-4 splits. A single vote can shape the law for generations. The Court's decisions aren't always unanimous, but the majority rules.

fragments.label: q054_fun
fragments.text: Five of the nine justices need to agree to make a ruling stick. But what if they tie 4-4? That happens when a seat is vacant or a justice steps aside. In that case, the lower court's decision is upheld — but no nationwide precedent is set. After Justice Scalia's death in 2016, several major cases ended in 4-4 ties.

fragments.label: q055_question
fragments.text: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?

fragments.label: q055_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q055_answer_1
fragments.text: (For) life

fragments.label: q055_answer_2
fragments.text: Lifetime appointment

fragments.label: q055_answer_3
fragments.text: (Until) retirement

fragments.label: q055_why
fragments.text: Supreme Court justices serve for life. They can leave only by resigning, retiring, or being impeached and removed. That makes their job unlike almost any other in government. They never have to run for re-election, never have to please voters or a president — they answer only to the Constitution.

fragments.label: q055_fun
fragments.text: Supreme Court justices keep their jobs for life — they can only be removed by impeachment. In 235+ years, only one Justice has ever been impeached: Samuel Chase, in 1804. The Senate acquitted him the next year, and he kept his seat. No Supreme Court justice has ever been removed from office. That's how secure 'life tenure' really is.

fragments.label: q056_question
fragments.text: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why?

fragments.label: q056_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q056_answer_1
fragments.text: To be independent (of politics)

fragments.label: q056_answer_2
fragments.text: To limit outside (political) influence

fragments.label: q056_why
fragments.text: Judicial independence is the whole point of life tenure. If justices could be fired for making unpopular rulings, they'd hesitate to defend the Constitution against angry presidents or powerful majorities. Serving for life means they can make tough calls based on the law — not on what's popular this year or which party is in power.

fragments.label: q056_fun
fragments.text: In Federalist 78, Alexander Hamilton called the judiciary 'the least dangerous branch' — judges have 'neither force nor will, but merely judgment.' They control no army, no budget. So why protect them with lifetime jobs? Because their only real power is to interpret the law fairly. If they could be fired for unpopular rulings, that power would be worthless.

fragments.label: q057_question
fragments.text: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?

fragments.label: q057_answer_1
fragments.text: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.

fragments.label: q057_why
fragments.text: The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court — the highest court in America. They preside when the Court hears cases, swear in the President at every inauguration, and lead the federal court system. It's a lifetime appointment, so a Chief Justice can shape American law for decades.

fragments.label: q057_fun
fragments.text: In the entire U.S. Constitution, the Chief Justice is mentioned by name just one time. Article I says: 'When the President of the United States is tried, the Chief Justice shall preside.' That's it. The most important judge in America is barely described in the founding document — almost everything about the role developed over time.

fragments.label: q058_question
fragments.text: Name one power that is only for the federal government.

fragments.label: q058_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q058_answer_1
fragments.text: Print paper money

fragments.label: q058_answer_2
fragments.text: Mint coins

fragments.label: q058_answer_3
fragments.text: Declare war

fragments.label: q058_answer_4
fragments.text: Create an army

fragments.label: q058_answer_5
fragments.text: Make treaties

fragments.label: q058_answer_6
fragments.text: Set foreign policy

fragments.label: q058_why
fragments.text: Some jobs only the federal government can do. One country needs one military, one currency, one set of foreign policies. Imagine if every state had its own army or printed its own money — the United States wouldn't really be united.

fragments.label: q058_fun
fragments.text: Before the Constitution, both Congress and each state printed their own paper money. The result was a mess — money from one state was often worthless in another. People joked that something useless was 'not worth a Continental,' which was the first paper money congress printed. The Constitution fixed this by giving only the federal government the power to print money.

fragments.label: q059_question
fragments.text: Name one power that is only for the states.

fragments.label: q059_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q059_answer_1
fragments.text: Provide schooling and education

fragments.label: q059_answer_2
fragments.text: Provide protection (police)

fragments.label: q059_answer_3
fragments.text: Provide safety (fire departments)

fragments.label: q059_answer_4
fragments.text: Give a driver's license

fragments.label: q059_answer_5
fragments.text: Approve zoning and land use

fragments.label: q059_why
fragments.text: Some powers stay with the states because local needs are different. A city in Wyoming faces different problems than New York City. The framers thought decisions about schools, police, and zoning should be made close to home — by people who actually live there — not by far-away officials in Washington.

fragments.label: q059_fun
fragments.text: Schools, police, and fire departments are state and local jobs — not federal. That's why a 2nd grader in Minnesota might read different books, learn different math methods, and take different tests than a 2nd grader in Florida. The U.S. has 50 separate state education systems and thousands of local school districts deciding what to teach.

fragments.label: q060_question
fragments.text: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?

fragments.label: q060_answer_1
fragments.text: (It states that the) powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.

fragments.label: q060_why
fragments.text: The 10th Amendment makes the basic rule of American government clear: the federal government has only the powers the Constitution gives it — nothing more. Everything else stays with the states, or with the people themselves.

fragments.label: q060_fun
fragments.text: The 10th Amendment is the last original amendment from the Bill of Rights — and it's the 'everything else' rule. Anti-Federalists worried the federal government would grab powers not on its list. The 10th flipped the assumption: if a power isn't given to Washington, it belongs to the states or the people.

fragments.label: q061_question
fragments.text: Who is the governor of your state now?

fragments.label: q061_answer_1
fragments.text: Answers will vary by state. (D.C. does not have a governor.)

fragments.label: q061_disambiguation
fragments.text: District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a governor.

fragments.label: q061_why
fragments.text: Your governor is the head of your state's executive branch — like a state-level president. They sign or veto state laws, command the state National Guard, and shape state policy on schools, roads, and taxes. State government touches your daily life far more often than the federal government does.

fragments.label: q061_fun
fragments.text: After the Revolution, Americans feared a strong governor might become another tyrant like King George. So most early state constitutions made governors very weak — chosen by the legislature, serving just one year, with no veto power. Today's governors, elected directly by voters for four-year terms, are far more powerful than the Founders intended.

fragments.label: q062_question
fragments.text: What is the capital of your state?

fragments.label: q062_answer_1
fragments.text: Saint Paul

fragments.label: q062_why
fragments.text: A state's capital is where state laws are made and state government runs. Saint Paul has been Minnesota's capital since 1849 — even before Minnesota became a state in 1858. Knowing your state capital connects you to the place where decisions about Minnesota's schools, roads, taxes, and laws actually get made.

fragments.label: q062_fun
fragments.text: The Minnesota State Capitol in Saint Paul was designed by Cass Gilbert, a young architect from St. Paul. He finished it in 1905. He did such a good job that 30 years later, he was hired to design an even bigger building: the U.S. Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C. Same architect, both buildings, marble and dome and all.

fragments.label: q063_question
fragments.text: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.

fragments.label: q063_lead_in
fragments.text: Pick any one of the four voting amendments and describe what it did:

fragments.label: q063_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens eighteen (18) and older (can vote).

fragments.label: q063_answer_2
fragments.text: You don't have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.

fragments.label: q063_answer_3
fragments.text: Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)

fragments.label: q063_answer_4
fragments.text: A male citizen of any race (can vote).

fragments.label: q063_disambiguation
fragments.text: The four voting amendments are the 15th (no race discrimination, 1870), the 19th (women, 1920), the 24th (no poll tax, 1964), and the 26th (age 18, 1971). You only need to describe one.

fragments.label: q063_why
fragments.text: When the Constitution was written, only white men who owned property could vote in most places. The right to vote has been expanded four times by amendment — for race, for women, against poll taxes, and for 18-year-olds. Each one made America a little more democratic. The work of including everyone took almost 200 years.

fragments.label: q063_fun
fragments.text: The 26th Amendment was ratified in just 100 days — faster than any other amendment in U.S. history. The push came from the Vietnam War: 18-year-olds were being drafted to fight but couldn't vote for the leaders who sent them. The slogan was 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote.' States agreed in record time.

fragments.label: q064_question
fragments.text: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?

fragments.label: q064_answer_1
fragments.text: Citizens

fragments.label: q064_answer_2
fragments.text: Citizens of the United States

fragments.label: q064_answer_3
fragments.text: U.S. citizens

fragments.label: q064_why
fragments.text: Some rights — like free speech and religion — belong to everyone in the United States. But three specific civic powers belong only to citizens: voting in federal elections, running for federal office, and serving on a jury. These are how citizens shape the government. They're the reason becoming a citizen matters.

fragments.label: q064_fun
fragments.text: After a person becomes a U.S. citizen through naturalization, they have nearly all the same rights as someone born here: voting, jury duty, running for Congress, even being a Supreme Court Justice. The Constitution sets aside just one job for natural-born citizens — President of the United States.

fragments.label: q065_question
fragments.text: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?

fragments.label: q065_lead_in
fragments.text: Pick any three of these (you need to name three):

fragments.label: q065_answer_1
fragments.text: Freedom of expression

fragments.label: q065_answer_2
fragments.text: Freedom of speech

fragments.label: q065_answer_3
fragments.text: Freedom of assembly

fragments.label: q065_answer_4
fragments.text: Freedom to petition the government

fragments.label: q065_answer_5
fragments.text: Freedom of religion

fragments.label: q065_answer_6
fragments.text: The right to bear arms

fragments.label: q065_disambiguation
fragments.text: The first five come from the First Amendment (religion, speech, press, assembly, petition). The right to bear arms comes from the Second Amendment. All of these apply to EVERYONE living in the U.S. — not just citizens.

fragments.label: q065_why
fragments.text: These rights belong to everyone living in the United States — citizens AND non-citizens. The framers chose words like 'the people' and 'persons,' not 'citizens.' That means the moment a person steps onto U.S. soil, they're protected by the Bill of Rights.

fragments.label: q065_fun
fragments.text: The First Amendment packs FIVE rights into one sentence: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. Most Americans can name only one or two when asked. And here's the key: these rights belong to EVERYONE living in the U.S. — not just citizens. The Bill of Rights talks about 'the people' and 'persons,' not just 'citizens.'

fragments.label: q066_question
fragments.text: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?

fragments.label: q066_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works:

fragments.label: q066_answer_1
fragments.text: The United States

fragments.label: q066_answer_2
fragments.text: The flag

fragments.label: q066_why
fragments.text: The Pledge is a public promise of loyalty to the United States and to its flag — the symbol that stands for the country. Saying it is a ritual that connects you to every American who has said the same words.

fragments.label: q066_fun
fragments.text: In 1943, during World War II, the Supreme Court ruled that no one in the U.S. can be forced to say the Pledge — even at school. Forcing someone to declare loyalty would violate the First Amendment. So when you say the Pledge, you're choosing to. Real loyalty is freely given, not commanded.

fragments.label: q067_question
fragments.text: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.

fragments.label: q067_lead_in
fragments.text: Name any two of these promises:

fragments.label: q067_answer_1
fragments.text: Give up loyalty to other countries

fragments.label: q067_answer_2
fragments.text: Defend the (U.S.) Constitution

fragments.label: q067_answer_3
fragments.text: Obey the laws of the United States

fragments.label: q067_answer_4
fragments.text: Serve in the military (if needed)

fragments.label: q067_answer_5
fragments.text: Serve (help, do important work for) the nation (if needed)

fragments.label: q067_answer_6
fragments.text: Be loyal to the United States

fragments.label: q067_why
fragments.text: The Oath is the final step of becoming a citizen — a public promise to defend the Constitution, obey U.S. laws, and put loyalty to the United States above any other country. It's not just paperwork. It's the moment a person stops being a guest in this country and starts being a member of it. From that moment on, this nation is theirs.

fragments.label: q067_fun
fragments.text: New citizens take their Oath of Allegiance at a public ceremony — at a courthouse, or sometimes inside the National Archives in front of the actual Constitution and Bill of Rights. A version of this oath has been said by new Americans since 1790. That's over 235 years of welcoming new citizens to the United States.

fragments.label: q068_question
fragments.text: How can people become United States citizens?

fragments.label: q068_lead_in
fragments.text: There are three ways. Any one is correct:

fragments.label: q068_answer_1
fragments.text: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment

fragments.label: q068_answer_2
fragments.text: Naturalize

fragments.label: q068_answer_3
fragments.text: Derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress)

fragments.label: q068_why
fragments.text: There are three paths to U.S. citizenship: being born here (under the 14th Amendment), going through naturalization (taking the Oath, like Q67), or deriving it from a parent who naturalizes. Most people become citizens just by being born; some choose it through years of paperwork and study. All three paths lead to the same status: full American citizen.

fragments.label: q068_fun
fragments.text: The 14th Amendment (1868) is the source of birthright citizenship. It was added right after the Civil War to overturn the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision (1857), which had ruled that Black people couldn't be U.S. citizens. The 14th made it constitutional law: anyone born in the U.S. is a citizen. Period.

fragments.label: q069_question
fragments.text: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?

fragments.label: q069_lead_in
fragments.text: Name any two of these forms of civic participation:

fragments.label: q069_answer_1
fragments.text: Vote

fragments.label: q069_answer_2
fragments.text: Run for office

fragments.label: q069_answer_3
fragments.text: Join a political party

fragments.label: q069_answer_4
fragments.text: Join a civic group

fragments.label: q069_answer_5
fragments.text: Join a community group

fragments.label: q069_answer_6
fragments.text: Give an elected official your opinion (on an issue)

fragments.label: q069_answer_7
fragments.text: Write to a newspaper

fragments.label: q069_why
fragments.text: American democracy doesn't just happen on election day. It happens when citizens join groups, contact their representatives, support causes, and speak up on issues. Voting is the most famous form, but it's only one of many. The Founders thought democracy needed citizens who actually participate — not just bystanders waiting for someone else to act.

fragments.label: q069_fun
fragments.text: In 1831, a French aristocrat named Alexis de Tocqueville toured America for 9 months. He was AMAZED at how Americans constantly formed groups for every cause — schools, churches, charities, political clubs. He called it 'the art of association' and said it was the secret of American democracy.

fragments.label: q070_question
fragments.text: What is one way Americans can serve their country?

fragments.label: q070_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these counts:

fragments.label: q070_answer_1
fragments.text: Vote

fragments.label: q070_answer_2
fragments.text: Pay taxes

fragments.label: q070_answer_3
fragments.text: Serve in the military

fragments.label: q070_answer_4
fragments.text: Run for office

fragments.label: q070_answer_5
fragments.text: Work for local, state, or federal government

fragments.label: q070_why
fragments.text: Serving your country doesn't only mean wearing a uniform. The Founders thought a republic couldn't survive unless ordinary citizens did their part: voting, paying taxes, obeying laws, helping their community. Service is what makes the whole system work. In a self-governing country, the citizens ARE the government — so they have to show up.

fragments.label: q070_fun
fragments.text: The Founders thought a republic couldn't survive unless citizens did their part. They called this 'civic virtue.' Service doesn't only mean joining the military — voting, paying taxes, even just obeying the law are all forms of service. They're what makes self-government actually work. A republic needs citizens who care enough to keep it running.

fragments.label: q071_question
fragments.text: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?

fragments.label: q071_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q071_answer_1
fragments.text: Required by law

fragments.label: q071_answer_2
fragments.text: Required by the (U.S.) Constitution (16th Amendment)

fragments.label: q071_answer_3
fragments.text: Civic duty

fragments.label: q071_why
fragments.text: Federal taxes pay for nearly everything the U.S. government does: the military, highways, Social Security, food safety, scientific research, federal courts. Without taxes, none of that works. Paying taxes is both a legal requirement (under the 16th Amendment) AND a basic way everyone helps fund the country.

fragments.label: q071_fun
fragments.text: For most of U.S. history, there was no federal income tax. The government paid for itself mostly with tariffs — taxes on imported goods. Then in 1895, the Supreme Court struck down a new income tax law. To get around that ruling, Congress and the states passed the 16th Amendment in 1913. That amendment is the reason your taxes get withheld today.

fragments.label: q072_question
fragments.text: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why.

fragments.label: q072_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these reasons works:

fragments.label: q072_answer_1
fragments.text: Required by law

fragments.label: q072_answer_2
fragments.text: Civic duty

fragments.label: q072_answer_3
fragments.text: Makes the draft fair, if needed

fragments.label: q072_why
fragments.text: Selective Service registration is a list of young men who could be called up if the U.S. ever needed a military draft. It's required by law for men 18-25, and the list makes sure that if a draft were ever needed, the burden would fall fairly across the population.

fragments.label: q072_fun
fragments.text: The U.S. hasn't actually used the draft since 1973 — over 50 years ago. The military today is all-volunteer. But every young man still has to register with Selective Service at 18, just in case.

fragments.label: q073_question
fragments.text: The colonists came to America for many reasons. Name one.

fragments.label: q073_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these reasons works:

fragments.label: q073_answer_1
fragments.text: Freedom

fragments.label: q073_answer_2
fragments.text: Political liberty

fragments.label: q073_answer_3
fragments.text: Religious freedom

fragments.label: q073_answer_4
fragments.text: Economic opportunity

fragments.label: q073_answer_5
fragments.text: Escape persecution

fragments.label: q073_why
fragments.text: The colonists didn't all come for one reason. Some wanted religious freedom, some wanted political liberty, some wanted economic opportunity, some were escaping persecution. That mix gave America its founding character: a country built by people who left somewhere else looking for something better. Most Americans today are still here for similar reasons.

fragments.label: q073_fun
fragments.text: The first English colonists came for completely different reasons. Jamestown (1607) was a business — investors hoped to find gold. The Pilgrims at Plymouth (1620) came for religious freedom. Pennsylvania was founded for religious tolerance. The 13 colonies had different personalities from day one.

fragments.label: q074_question
fragments.text: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?

fragments.label: q074_lead_in
fragments.text: Either name works:

fragments.label: q074_answer_1
fragments.text: American Indians

fragments.label: q074_answer_2
fragments.text: Native Americans

fragments.label: q074_why
fragments.text: Native Americans had been living across North America for thousands of years before any European arrived. They had hundreds of distinct nations, languages, cultures, and governments. Acknowledging this is part of telling American history honestly.

fragments.label: q074_fun
fragments.text: Native Americans had been here for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. They had complex governments — the Iroquois Confederacy had its own constitution, the Great Law of Peace, that worked for centuries. Benjamin Franklin studied it. In 1988, Congress officially recognized that the Iroquois helped shape the U.S. Constitution.

fragments.label: q075_question
fragments.text: What group of people was taken and sold as slaves?

fragments.label: q075_lead_in
fragments.text: Either answer works:

fragments.label: q075_answer_1
fragments.text: Africans

fragments.label: q075_answer_2
fragments.text: People from Africa

fragments.label: q075_why
fragments.text: Millions of people were taken from Africa and forced into slavery in the Americas. In the United States, slavery lasted from 1619 until 1865 — over 240 years. American freedom and prosperity were built, in part, on the unfree labor of enslaved people. Facing this honestly is part of being an American.

fragments.label: q075_fun
fragments.text: The first Africans were brought to Jamestown, Virginia in 1619.  Ending it required a civil war that killed more Americans than any other war in our history.

fragments.label: q076_question
fragments.text: What war did the Americans fight to win independence from Britain?

fragments.label: q076_lead_in
fragments.text: Any of these names works:

fragments.label: q076_answer_1
fragments.text: American Revolution

fragments.label: q076_answer_2
fragments.text: The (American) Revolutionary War

fragments.label: q076_answer_3
fragments.text: War for (American) Independence

fragments.label: q076_why
fragments.text: The American Revolution made the United States a country. Thirteen colonies — small and divided — defeated the most powerful empire on Earth and created a new kind of government, based on the idea that ordinary people could govern themselves. Every freedom Americans have today traces back to this war.

fragments.label: q076_fun
fragments.text: The Revolutionary War lasted 8 years (1775-1783). It wasn't just America vs. Britain — it was also a civil war. About 20-30% of colonists stayed loyal to the king and fought against the patriots. After the war, around 60,000 Loyalists fled the U.S. for Canada and other places. Independence split families and neighbors.

fragments.label: q077_question
fragments.text: Name one reason why the Americans declared independence from Britain.

fragments.label: q077_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these reasons works (you only need one):

fragments.label: q077_answer_1
fragments.text: Taxation without representation

fragments.label: q077_answer_2
fragments.text: They did not have self-government

fragments.label: q077_answer_3
fragments.text: Boston Massacre

fragments.label: q077_answer_4
fragments.text: Boston Tea Party (Tea Act)

fragments.label: q077_why
fragments.text: The Americans didn't break away over a single thing, it was years of frustration: taxes they couldn't vote on, soldiers in their houses, laws they had no say in. The deepest reason was a principle: a free people should govern themselves. When Britain refused to listen, the colonists decided to make their own country. That principle still anchors America.

fragments.label: q077_fun
fragments.text: On the night of December 16, 1773, about 100 colonists disguised as Mohawk Indians snuck onto British ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of tea overboard. The protest had a slogan: 'No taxation without representation.' Britain's furious response — the Intolerable Acts — pushed the colonies one step closer to revolution.

fragments.label: q078_question
fragments.text: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?

fragments.label: q078_answer_1
fragments.text: (Thomas) Jefferson

fragments.label: q078_why
fragments.text: Thomas Jefferson, then 33 years old, wrote the Declaration of Independence in a few weeks in a rented Philadelphia room. His words — 'all men are created equal,' the right to 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' — became the founding promise of the United States. America has spent its whole history trying to live up to that promise.

fragments.label: q078_fun
fragments.text: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration at age 33. Fifty years later, on July 4, 1826 — the EXACT 50th anniversary of the Declaration — Jefferson and John Adams both died on the same day. Adams was the last to go; his final words: 'Thomas Jefferson survives.' But Jefferson had died hours earlier.

fragments.label: q079_question
fragments.text: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?

fragments.label: q079_answer_1
fragments.text: July 4, 1776

fragments.label: q079_why
fragments.text: July 4, 1776 is the day the Continental Congress officially adopted the Declaration of Independence. It marks the moment 13 colonies stopped being British subjects and declared themselves a new nation. Every July 4 since has been celebrated as the country's birthday.

fragments.label: q079_fun
fragments.text: July 4, 1776 is when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration's text — but most delegates didn't actually sign it until August 2. So Independence Day celebrates the day we voted, not the day we signed.

fragments.label: q080_question
fragments.text: The American Revolution had many important events. Name one.

fragments.label: q080_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q080_answer_1
fragments.text: (Battle of) Bunker Hill

fragments.label: q080_answer_2
fragments.text: Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q080_answer_3
fragments.text: Washington Crossing the Delaware (Battle of Trenton)

fragments.label: q080_why
