fragments.text: The Revolution wasn't won in a single battle. It was years of small victories, brutal defeats, and near-disasters. Bunker Hill proved Americans could fight. The Declaration of Independence gave them a reason to fight. Saratoga and Valley Forge tested whether they could keep fighting. Yorktown finally won the war.

fragments.label: q080_fun
fragments.text: On Christmas night 1776, Washington led 2,400 freezing soldiers across the icy Delaware River in a snowstorm. They marched 9 miles to surprise the Hessians (German mercenary fighters) soldiers at Trenton early the next morning. The Continental Army was nearly destroyed at that point. The victory saved the Revolution.

fragments.label: q081_question
fragments.text: There were 13 original states. Name five.

fragments.label: q081_lead_in
fragments.text: Name any FIVE of the 13 original states:

fragments.label: q081_answer_1
fragments.text: New York

fragments.label: q081_answer_2
fragments.text: New Jersey

fragments.label: q081_answer_3
fragments.text: Massachusetts

fragments.label: q081_answer_4
fragments.text: Pennsylvania

fragments.label: q081_answer_5
fragments.text: Maryland

fragments.label: q081_answer_6
fragments.text: Virginia

fragments.label: q081_answer_7
fragments.text: Georgia

fragments.label: q081_answer_8
fragments.text: Delaware

fragments.label: q081_answer_9
fragments.text: North Carolina

fragments.label: q081_answer_10
fragments.text: South Carolina

fragments.label: q081_answer_11
fragments.text: New Hampshire

fragments.label: q081_answer_12
fragments.text: Rhode Island

fragments.label: q081_answer_13
fragments.text: Connecticut

fragments.label: q081_why
fragments.text: The 13 original states were the first members of the United States. Each was a separate colony that fought together in the Revolution and then agreed to form one country. The 13 stripes on the U.S. flag still honor them today.

fragments.label: q081_fun
fragments.text: Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution — December 7, 1787, by a unanimous 30-0 vote. That's why its nickname is 'The First State.' Rhode Island was DEAD LAST — May 29, 1790, almost 3 years later. Rhode Island only agreed after Congress threatened to treat it as a foreign country.

fragments.label: q082_question
fragments.text: What founding document was written in 1787?

fragments.label: q082_answer_1
fragments.text: (U.S.) Constitution

fragments.label: q082_why
fragments.text: The Constitution was written in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and is still the supreme law of the land today — over 235 years later. It's the oldest written national constitution still in use anywhere in the world. Every American law, every court ruling, every action of the federal government has to fit within it.

fragments.label: q082_fun
fragments.text: The Convention was called in 1787 just to fix the broken Articles of Confederation. Instead, the delegates secretly threw the Articles out and wrote a brand-new Constitution. They kept the windows closed in summer heat so no one outside could hear. They knew they were exceeding their authority — and did it anyway.

fragments.label: q083_question
fragments.text: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.

fragments.label: q083_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q083_answer_1
fragments.text: (James) Madison

fragments.label: q083_answer_2
fragments.text: (Alexander) Hamilton

fragments.label: q083_answer_3
fragments.text: (John) Jay

fragments.label: q083_answer_4
fragments.text: Publius

fragments.label: q083_why
fragments.text: The Federalist Papers were 85 newspaper essays written in 1787-88 by three of America's sharpest political minds to convince New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution. They worked. New York approved. Today these essays are still the most important explanation of what the Constitution means — the Supreme Court cites them more than any other historical source.

fragments.label: q083_fun
fragments.text: All 85 essays were published under one pen name: Publius. The real authors did very different shares of the work — Alexander Hamilton wrote 51 essays, James Madison wrote 29, and John Jay wrote only 5. Hamilton did more than half by himself.

fragments.label: q084_question
fragments.text: Why were the Federalist Papers important?

fragments.label: q084_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q084_answer_1
fragments.text: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.

fragments.label: q084_answer_2
fragments.text: They supported passing the (U.S.) Constitution.

fragments.label: q084_why
fragments.text: The Federalist Papers turned a brand-new, untested document into something Americans could trust. They explained, defended, and argued for the Constitution — clause by clause — when the country was deciding whether to adopt it.

fragments.label: q084_fun
fragments.text: James Madison wrote one of the most famous lines in American political thought in Federalist 51: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.' In just 9 words, he explained the whole point of the Constitution — because people aren't perfect, the government needs checks and balances to control itself too.

fragments.label: q085_question
fragments.text: Benjamin Franklin is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q085_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q085_answer_1
fragments.text: Founded the first free public libraries

fragments.label: q085_answer_2
fragments.text: First Postmaster General of the United States

fragments.label: q085_answer_3
fragments.text: Helped write the Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q085_answer_4
fragments.text: Inventor

fragments.label: q085_answer_5
fragments.text: U.S. diplomat

fragments.label: q085_why
fragments.text: Benjamin Franklin did the work of about five different careers — printer, scientist, inventor, diplomat, and statesman — all in one lifetime. He invented bifocal glasses, the lightning rod, and the Franklin stove. He convinced France to enter the Revolution on America's side. He was 81 at the Constitutional Convention, the oldest delegate.

fragments.label: q085_fun
fragments.text: Benjamin Franklin signed all four documents that built the United States: the Declaration of Independence (1776), the Treaty of Alliance with France (1778), the Treaty of Paris ending the Revolution (1783), and the Constitution (1787). He's the only Founding Father to put his name on every one of them.

fragments.label: q086_question
fragments.text: George Washington is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q086_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q086_answer_1
fragments.text: "Father of Our Country"

fragments.label: q086_answer_2
fragments.text: First president of the United States

fragments.label: q086_answer_3
fragments.text: General of the Continental Army

fragments.label: q086_answer_4
fragments.text: President of the Constitutional Convention

fragments.label: q086_why
fragments.text: George Washington led the Continental Army through 8 years of war, presided over the Constitutional Convention, then became the first President. He set the precedents every president has followed since — including stepping down after 2 terms when he could have stayed in power. He's called the Father of Our Country.

fragments.label: q086_fun
fragments.text: In 1782, an army officer wrote George Washington suggesting he become King of the new country. Washington wrote back instantly, saying he viewed the idea 'with abhorrence' — that no event in the entire war had given him 'more painful sensations.' The man who could have been America's king chose to become its citizen instead.

fragments.label: q087_question
fragments.text: Thomas Jefferson is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q087_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q087_answer_1
fragments.text: Writer of the Declaration of Independence

fragments.label: q087_answer_2
fragments.text: Third president of the United States

fragments.label: q087_answer_3
fragments.text: Doubled the size of the United States (Louisiana Purchase)

fragments.label: q087_answer_4
fragments.text: First Secretary of State

fragments.label: q087_answer_5
fragments.text: Founded the University of Virginia

fragments.label: q087_answer_6
fragments.text: Writer of the Virginia Statute on Religious Freedom

fragments.label: q087_why
fragments.text: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first Secretary of State, became the third President, and doubled the size of the country through the Louisiana Purchase, which expanded land from 15 new states. He wrote Virginia's law guaranteeing religious freedom — which later became the model for the First Amendment.

fragments.label: q087_fun
fragments.text: Thomas Jefferson designed his own gravestone and listed exactly 3 things he wanted to be remembered for: writer of the Declaration of Independence, writer of the Virginia Statute on Religious Freedom, and founder of the University of Virginia. He said 'not a word more.' He didn't even mention being President.

fragments.label: q088_question
fragments.text: James Madison is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q088_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q088_answer_1
fragments.text: "Father of the Constitution"

fragments.label: q088_answer_2
fragments.text: Fourth president of the United States

fragments.label: q088_answer_3
fragments.text: President during the War of 1812

fragments.label: q088_answer_4
fragments.text: One of the writers of the Federalist Papers

fragments.label: q088_why
fragments.text: James Madison was the architect of the Constitution — he arrived at the 1787 Convention with a plan ready, helped write the document, then drafted the Bill of Rights to add 10 protections for individual freedoms. He went on to be the fourth President and led the country through the War of 1812. He's called the Father of the Constitution.

fragments.label: q088_fun
fragments.text: James Madison kept secret notes every single day of the Constitutional Convention. He never published them in his lifetime — they came out in 1840, four years after he died. Without those notes, we wouldn't know what happened in that closed-windows summer of 1787.

fragments.label: q089_question
fragments.text: Alexander Hamilton is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q089_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q089_answer_1
fragments.text: First Secretary of the Treasury

fragments.label: q089_answer_2
fragments.text: One of the writers of the Federalist Papers

fragments.label: q089_answer_3
fragments.text: Helped establish the First Bank of the United States

fragments.label: q089_answer_4
fragments.text: Aide to General George Washington

fragments.label: q089_answer_5
fragments.text: Member of the Continental Congress

fragments.label: q089_why
fragments.text: Alexander Hamilton built the U.S. financial system from scratch — as the first Secretary of the Treasury, he created the national bank, set up the currency, and figured out how to pay off the country's war debts. He was Washington's right-hand officer during the Revolution and wrote most of the Federalist Papers defending the new Constitution.

fragments.label: q089_fun
fragments.text: Alexander Hamilton was born poor on the tiny Caribbean island of Nevis — he was an illegitimate child orphaned at 11. At 17, he wrote so beautifully that townspeople raised money to send him to America for an education. He arrived in New York with nothing and went on to create the U.S. financial system from scratch.

fragments.label: q090_question
fragments.text: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?

fragments.label: q090_answer_1
fragments.text: Louisiana Territory

fragments.label: q090_answer_2
fragments.text: Louisiana

fragments.label: q090_why
fragments.text: In 1803, the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France — 828,000 square miles of land stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains. The deal DOUBLED the size of the country in one stroke and eventually became all or part of 15 states. It was the largest land deal in American history.

fragments.label: q090_fun
fragments.text: American negotiators went to Paris in 1803 just to buy the city of New Orleans. Napoleon, was desperate for money to fight Britain, and surprised Thomas Jefferson by offering the entire Louisiana Territory: 828,000 square miles for $15 million, about 4 cents an acre. Jefferson said yes on the spot, exceeding his instructions. The deal doubled the size of the country overnight.

fragments.label: q091_question
fragments.text: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.

fragments.label: q091_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q091_answer_1
fragments.text: War of 1812

fragments.label: q091_answer_2
fragments.text: Mexican-American War

fragments.label: q091_answer_3
fragments.text: Civil War

fragments.label: q091_answer_4
fragments.text: Spanish-American War

fragments.label: q091_why
fragments.text: The 1800s were the wars of America's adolescence. The War of 1812 with Britain proved the new country could defend itself. The Mexican-American War in the 1840s expanded the country to the Pacific. The Civil War nearly tore it apart. The Spanish-American War in 1898 made the U.S. a world power. Each one reshaped what America was.

fragments.label: q091_fun
fragments.text: In August 1814, during the War of 1812, British soldiers marched into Washington and burned the White House and the Capitol. First Lady Dolley Madison stayed in the burning city long enough to save the famous Stuart portrait of George Washington from the wall — then fled. The next day a tornado swept through and put out the fires.

fragments.label: q092_question
fragments.text: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.

fragments.label: q092_answer_1
fragments.text: The Civil War

fragments.label: q092_why
fragments.text: The Civil War (1861-1865) was the war that decided whether the United States would remain one country and whether slavery would survive in it. The North won. The Union held together. Slavery was ended by the 13th Amendment. Without the Civil War, there might not be a United States today, and millions of people would have remained enslaved.

fragments.label: q092_fun
fragments.text: At least 620,000 Americans died in the Civil War, about 2% of the country's population at the time. If the same percentage died in a war today, the death toll would be over 6 million. More Americans died in the Civil War than in World War I, World War II, Korea, and Vietnam combined.

fragments.label: q093_question
fragments.text: The Civil War had many important events. Name one.

fragments.label: q093_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q093_answer_1
fragments.text: Emancipation Proclamation

fragments.label: q093_answer_2
fragments.text: (Battle of) Gettysburg

fragments.label: q093_answer_3
fragments.text: Sherman's March

fragments.label: q093_answer_4
fragments.text: (Surrender at) Appomattox

fragments.label: q093_answer_5
fragments.text: Lincoln was assassinated.

fragments.label: q093_why
fragments.text: The Civil War lasted 4 years and changed everything about the country. Fort Sumter started it. Gettysburg and Vicksburg turned the tide. The Emancipation Proclamation made it a war against slavery. Sherman's March broke the Confederacy. Appomattox ended it. Lincoln's assassination cast a shadow over the peace. Each event mattered.

fragments.label: q093_fun
fragments.text: When General Lee from the Sourthern Confederate Army surrendered to General Grant of the Northern Union Army at Appomattox in April 1865, Grant gave shockingly generous terms: Confederate officers could kept their sidearms, soldiers kept their horses to plant spring crops, and Lee left wearing his sword. After 4 years of brutal war, Grant chose grace over revenge — and helped a torn country begin to come back together.

fragments.label: q094_question
fragments.text: Abraham Lincoln is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q094_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q094_answer_1
fragments.text: Freed the slaves (Emancipation Proclamation)

fragments.label: q094_answer_2
fragments.text: Saved (or preserved) the Union

fragments.label: q094_answer_3
fragments.text: Led the United States during the Civil War

fragments.label: q094_answer_4
fragments.text: 16th president of the United States

fragments.label: q094_answer_5
fragments.text: Delivered the Gettysburg Address

fragments.label: q094_why
fragments.text: Abraham Lincoln held the country together during its worst crisis. He led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation to end slavery, and gave the Gettysburg Address. He was assassinated 5 days after the war ended — the first U.S. president killed in office.

fragments.label: q094_fun
fragments.text: The main speaker at Gettysburg, Edward Everett, spoke for two hours. Then President Lincoln rose and spoke for two minutes — just 272 words. Everett wrote Lincoln the next day, admitting he wished he'd captured the meaning of the day in 2 hours as well as Lincoln did in 2. The speech became one of the greatest in American history.

fragments.label: q095_question
fragments.text: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?

fragments.label: q095_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q095_answer_1
fragments.text: Freed the slaves

fragments.label: q095_answer_2
fragments.text: Freed slaves in the Confederacy

fragments.label: q095_answer_3
fragments.text: Freed slaves in the Confederate states

fragments.label: q095_answer_4
fragments.text: Freed slaves in most Southern states

fragments.label: q095_why
fragments.text: President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863. It declared that enslaved people in the Confederate states were free, and it transformed the Civil War from a war to save the Union into a war to also end slavery. It opened the door for Black men to fight in the Union Army. Final, full abolition came with the 13th Amendment in 1865.

fragments.label: q095_fun
fragments.text: The Emancipation Proclamation didn't free every enslaved person — only those in the 10 Confederate states still in rebellion. Over 500,000 people stayed enslaved in border states like Kentucky and Maryland. News didn't reach 250,000 enslaved people in Texas until June 19, 1865 — that day became Juneteenth, now a federal holiday.

fragments.label: q096_question
fragments.text: What U.S. war ended slavery?

fragments.label: q096_answer_1
fragments.text: The Civil War

fragments.label: q096_why
fragments.text: The Civil War ended slavery in the United States. The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) began the process; the Union victory in 1865 enforced it; the 13th Amendment (also 1865) made it permanent and applied to everyone, everywhere in the country. It took 246 years of slavery and 4 years of war to reach the simple truth: no human should own another.

fragments.label: q096_fun
fragments.text: By the end of the Civil War, about 180,000 Black soldiers had served in the Union Army — roughly 1 in every 10 Union soldiers. More than half had been enslaved before the war and were fighting for their own freedom. Their service helped earn African American men the right to vote with the 15th Amendment in 1870.

fragments.label: q097_question
fragments.text: What amendment says all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are U.S. citizens?

fragments.label: q097_answer_1
fragments.text: 14th Amendment

fragments.label: q097_why
fragments.text: The 14th Amendment (1868) established birthright citizenship — anyone born here is a U.S. citizen. It also guarantees 'equal protection of the laws' to every person. This amendment has been used to end school segregation, protect interracial marriage, and expand civil rights for 150+ years. It's one of the most powerful sentences in American law.

fragments.label: q097_fun
fragments.text: In 1857, the Supreme Court ruled in Dred Scott v. Sandford that Black people — enslaved OR free — could never be U.S. citizens. Many legal scholars call it the worst Supreme Court decision in American history. The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868, said the opposite: anyone born in the U.S. is a citizen, regardless of race.

fragments.label: q098_question
fragments.text: When did all men get the right to vote?

fragments.label: q098_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q098_answer_1
fragments.text: After the Civil War

fragments.label: q098_answer_2
fragments.text: During Reconstruction

fragments.label: q098_answer_3
fragments.text: (With the) 15th Amendment

fragments.label: q098_why
fragments.text: The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870, said states could not deny anyone the right to vote based on race or 'previous condition of servitude.' For the first time, Black men could legally vote. But Southern states blocked them in practice — using poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence for nearly 100 years, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

fragments.label: q098_fun
fragments.text: The 15th Amendment was ratified February 3, 1870, giving Black men the legal right to vote. Just 22 days later, Hiram Revels of Mississippi was sworn in as the first Black U.S. Senator. One activist called him 'the Fifteenth Amendment in flesh and blood.'

fragments.label: q099_question
fragments.text: Name one leader of the women's rights movement in the 1800s.

fragments.label: q099_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q099_answer_1
fragments.text: Susan B. Anthony

fragments.label: q099_answer_2
fragments.text: Harriet Tubman

fragments.label: q099_answer_3
fragments.text: Elizabeth Cady Stanton

fragments.label: q099_answer_4
fragments.text: Sojourner Truth

fragments.label: q099_answer_5
fragments.text: Lucretia Mott

fragments.label: q099_answer_6
fragments.text: Lucy Stone

fragments.label: q099_why
fragments.text: Women's rights leaders in the 1800s fought for the right to vote, own property, sign contracts, attend college, and be considered equal under the law. The movement began at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848. It took 72 more years — and the work of generations of women — before the 19th Amendment finally gave women the right to vote in 1920.

fragments.label: q099_fun
fragments.text: Susan B. Anthony VOTED in the 1872 Presidential election in Rochester, NY — and was ARRESTED for it. Convicted and fined $100, she refused to pay; the government never collected. She died in 1906 — 14 YEARS before the 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote. She fought her whole life for a right she'd never use.

fragments.label: q100_question
fragments.text: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.

fragments.label: q100_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q100_answer_1
fragments.text: World War I

fragments.label: q100_answer_2
fragments.text: World War II

fragments.label: q100_answer_3
fragments.text: Korean War

fragments.label: q100_answer_4
fragments.text: Vietnam War

fragments.label: q100_answer_5
fragments.text: (Persian) Gulf War

fragments.label: q100_why
fragments.text: The 1900s were the most warring century in American history. The U.S. fought 5 major wars: WWI (1917-1918) and WWII (1941-1945) made America a world power. Korea (1950-1953) and Vietnam (1955-1975) were Cold War conflicts to stop communism. The Persian Gulf War (1990-1991) defended Kuwait from Iraq. Each shaped the country in lasting ways.

fragments.label: q100_fun
fragments.text: World War I ended at the 11th hour of the 11th DAY of the 11th month — November 11, 1918, at 11:00 AM. Americans celebrated that date as Armistice Day for decades. After World War II and Korea, Congress renamed it Veterans Day in 1954 to honor everyone who's served. That's why Veterans Day is November 11.

fragments.label: q101_question
fragments.text: Why did the United States enter World War I?

fragments.label: q101_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q101_answer_1
fragments.text: Because Germany attacked U.S. (civilian) ships

fragments.label: q101_answer_2
fragments.text: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, Italy, and Russia)

fragments.label: q101_answer_3
fragments.text: To oppose the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria)

fragments.label: q101_why
fragments.text: World War I started in 1914 between European nations. The United States stayed out for 3 years. But Germany began sinking American ships with submarines, and a secret German plot to recruit Mexico against the U.S. tipped public opinion. America declared war on April 6, 1917. U.S. troops helped end the war 19 months later in November 1918.

fragments.label: q101_fun
fragments.text: In January 1917, Germany sent a secret coded message to Mexico: join Germany against the U.S., and Germany would help Mexico get back Texas, Arizona, and New Mexico (lost in 1848). British spies intercepted and decoded it. When Americans learned the contents, public outrage tipped the country into World War I.

fragments.label: q102_question
fragments.text: When did all women get the right to vote?

fragments.label: q102_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q102_answer_2
fragments.text: After World War I

fragments.label: q102_answer_3
fragments.text: (With the) 19th Amendment

fragments.label: q102_why
fragments.text: The 19th Amendment (1920) gave American women the right to vote. It came 72 years after the Seneca Falls Convention started the movement. About 26 million women became eligible overnight. Black women in the South still faced poll taxes and intimidation — the right wasn't fully real until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

fragments.label: q102_fun
fragments.text: The 19th Amendment needed 36 states to ratify. Tennessee was state 36. The Tennessee House was deadlocked 48-48. Then 24-year-old Harry Burn opened a letter from his mother: 'Be a good boy and help Mrs. Catt put the rat in ratification.' Harry switched his vote to YES. American women won the right to vote because a mom wrote her son.

fragments.label: q103_question
fragments.text: What was the Great Depression?

fragments.label: q103_answer_1
fragments.text: Longest economic recession in modern history

fragments.label: q103_why
fragments.text: The Great Depression lasted ten years, from 1929 to 1939. It was the worst economic collapse in modern history. Businesses closed by the hundreds of thousands. Banks failed. Millions of Americans lost their jobs, savings, and homes. The country never forgot it.

fragments.label: q103_fun
fragments.text: At its worst in 1933, one in four American workers had no job. Nearly 10,000 banks failed — wiping out the life savings of 9 million Americans. The Great Depression was so devastating that it permanently changed what Americans expected from their government — leading to Social Security, bank deposit insurance, and minimum wage laws.

fragments.label: q104_question
fragments.text: When did the Great Depression start?

fragments.label: q104_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q104_answer_1
fragments.text: The Great Crash (1929)

fragments.label: q104_answer_2
fragments.text: Stock market crash of 1929

fragments.label: q104_why
fragments.text: The Great Depression started with the Stock Market Crash of October 1929. Stock prices had been rising for years, fueled by people borrowing money to buy more stocks. When prices started falling, panic spread. Banks that had also invested in stocks failed. People lost their savings. Within 3 years, the entire economy had collapsed.

fragments.label: q104_fun
fragments.text: The Stock Market Crash of 1929 wiped out nearly 90% of the Dow Jones index by 1932. People who'd invested $100 in stocks had about $10 left. The Dow didn't recover its 1929 peak until 1954 — twenty five years later.

fragments.label: q105_question
fragments.text: Who was president during the Great Depression and World War II?

fragments.label: q105_answer_1
fragments.text: (Franklin) Roosevelt

fragments.label: q105_why
fragments.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) became president in 1933 and served until his death in 1945 — leading the country through its two biggest crises: the Great Depression and WWII. His New Deal programs (Social Security, FDIC, public works) reshaped what Americans expected from their government. He died less than a month before Nazi Germany surrendered.

fragments.label: q105_fun
fragments.text: Franklin Roosevelt is the only president ever elected to four terms (1932, 1936, 1940, 1944). After he died in office, Congress passed the 22nd Amendment in 1951 limiting future presidents to 2 terms — his record can never be broken. He led the country through the Depression and WWII while paralyzed by polio from the waist down.

fragments.label: q106_question
fragments.text: Why did the United States enter World War II?

fragments.label: q106_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q106_answer_1
fragments.text: (Bombing of) Pearl Harbor

fragments.label: q106_answer_2
fragments.text: Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor

fragments.label: q106_answer_3
fragments.text: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, and Russia)

fragments.label: q106_answer_4
fragments.text: To oppose the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, and Japan)

fragments.label: q106_why
fragments.text: America stayed out of WWII for over 2 years while Germany conquered Europe and Japan attacked Asia. That changed on December 7, 1941, when Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The next day, FDR called it 'a date which will live in infamy' and asked Congress for war.

fragments.label: q106_fun
fragments.text: On December 7, 1941, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor lasted under 2 hours but killed over 2,300 Americans. The battleship USS Arizona sank with 1,177 sailors aboard. More than 900 are still entombed inside the wreck today — a war grave you can visit at the Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor.

fragments.label: q107_question
fragments.text: Dwight Eisenhower is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q107_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q107_answer_1
fragments.text: General during World War II

fragments.label: q107_answer_2
fragments.text: President at the end of (during) the Korean War

fragments.label: q107_answer_3
fragments.text: 34th president of the United States

fragments.label: q107_answer_4
fragments.text: Signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Created the Interstate System)

fragments.label: q107_why
fragments.text: Eisenhower had two of America's biggest jobs in 12 years. As General, he commanded the D-Day invasion of Europe in 1944 — the largest amphibious war operation in history — that helped defeat Nazi Germany. Then as 34th president (1953-61), he ended the Korean War, built the Interstate Highway System, and warned Americans about the 'military-industrial complex.'

fragments.label: q107_fun
fragments.text: Eisenhower's Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 created the U.S. Interstate Highway System — but its official name was the National Interstate and defense Highways Act. It was a national security project: highways to move troops fast in case of war. The 47,000-mile system Americans drive on every day is now named the Eisenhower Interstate System.

fragments.label: q108_question
fragments.text: Who was the United States' main rival during the Cold War?

fragments.label: q108_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q108_answer_1
fragments.text: Soviet Union

fragments.label: q108_answer_2
fragments.text: USSR

fragments.label: q108_answer_3
fragments.text: Russia

fragments.label: q108_why
fragments.text: The Soviet Union (USSR) was the world's other superpower after WWII. From 1947 to 1991, the U.S. and USSR competed for global influence without ever fighting each other directly. Both built thousands of nuclear weapons, fought 'proxy wars' in Korea, Vietnam, and Afghanistan, as well as the space race. The USSR collapsed in 1991, splitting into 15 countries.

fragments.label: q108_fun
fragments.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik — the first artificial satellite, no bigger than a beach ball. Americans PANICKED: if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, they could put a nuclear missile anywhere on Earth. Within 9 months, the U.S. founded NASA. The space race was on. We won it by landing on the Moon in 1969.

fragments.label: q109_question
fragments.text: During the Cold War, what was one main concern of the United States?

fragments.label: q109_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q109_answer_1
fragments.text: Communism

fragments.label: q109_answer_2
fragments.text: Nuclear war

fragments.label: q109_why
fragments.text: The Cold War (1947-1991) was a 44-year rivalry between the U.S. and Soviet Union. The two sides never fought directly, but they built terrifying nuclear weapons stockpiles. At the peak in the 1980s, the world held over 70,000 nuclear weapons.

fragments.label: q109_fun
fragments.text: For 13 days in October 1962, the world stood on the edge of nuclear war. The Soviets had secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba — just 90 miles from Florida. They could hit American cities in under 5 minutes. President Kennedy demanded their removal. Both sides backed down at the last moment. The closest the Cold War ever came to actual nuclear war.

fragments.label: q110_question
fragments.text: Why did the United States enter the Korean War?

fragments.label: q110_answer_1
fragments.text: To stop the spread of communism

fragments.label: q110_why
fragments.text: After WWII, Korea was split into a communist North (backed by USSR and China) and an American-backed South. In 1950, North Korea invaded the South. The U.S. led a UN coalition to defend South Korea. About 36,000 Americans died over 3 years. The war ended where it began: with Korea divided at the 38th parallel.

fragments.label: q110_fun
fragments.text: The Korean War (1950-53) ended with an armistice — not a peace treaty. North and South Korea are still technically at war today. The war split one Korean nation into two opposite worlds: South Korea became a thriving democracy and major economy with companies like Samsung, and the K-pop music industry. North Korea is one of the most isolated countries on Earth.

fragments.label: q111_question
fragments.text: Why did the United States enter the Vietnam War?

fragments.label: q111_answer_1
fragments.text: To stop the spread of communism

fragments.label: q111_why
fragments.text: After WWII, Vietnam was a French colony fighting for independence. When France lost in 1954, Vietnam split. The North became communist North and The United States backed the democratic South. The U.S. sent troops in 1965 to stop communism spreading. The war became deeply unpopular at home. Over 58,000 Americans died. The U.S. withdrew in 1973 and the communist North captured the South in 1975.

fragments.label: q111_fun
fragments.text: The Vietnam War was America's longest war up to that point — about 20 years of involvement. Over 58,000 Americans died. When the U.S. pulled out and North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon on April 30, 1975, the communist North won. The country is still ruled by communists today.

fragments.label: q112_question
fragments.text: What did the civil rights movement do?

fragments.label: q112_answer_1
fragments.text: Fought to end racial discrimination

fragments.label: q112_why
fragments.text: The civil rights movement (roughly 1954-1968) used nonviolent protest, lawsuits, and moral persuasion to dismantle America's system of racial segregation, which means social practices to keep black citizens separate. It won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (banning segregation in public places) and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (finally enforcing what the 15th Amendment promised in 1870).

fragments.label: q112_fun
fragments.text: On December 1, 1955, 42-year-old Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. She was arrested. The Black community organized a bus boycott — they walked and carpooled for 381 DAYS. The Supreme Court ended bus segregation. The boycott introduced the world to a 26-year-old minister: Martin Luther King Jr.

fragments.label: q113_question
fragments.text: Martin Luther King, Jr. is famous for many things. Name one.

fragments.label: q113_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q113_answer_1
fragments.text: Fighting for civil rights

fragments.label: q113_answer_2
fragments.text: Working for equality for all Americans

fragments.label: q113_answer_3
fragments.text: Working to ensure that people would 'not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character'

fragments.label: q113_why
fragments.text: Martin Luther King Jr. led the civil rights movement using nonviolent protest, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi. He delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech (1963), won the Nobel Peace Prize at age 35 (1964), and was assassinated in 1968 at age 39. He is the only individual American with his own federal holiday besides George Washington.

fragments.label: q113_fun
fragments.text: On August 28, 1963, Martin Luther King stood before 250,000 people at the Lincoln Memorial. He was reading from a prepared text when gospel singer Mahalia Jackson shouted: 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' He set aside his notes and improvised the most famous passage in American oratory: 'I have a dream...'

fragments.label: q114_question
fragments.text: Why did the United States enter the Persian Gulf War?

fragments.label: q114_answer_1
fragments.text: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait

fragments.label: q114_why
fragments.text: On August 2, 1990, Iraq invaded its small oil-rich neighbor Kuwait. President George H.W. Bush assembled a 35-nation coalition under the United Nations to push Iraq out. After 5 weeks of air strikes and a brief ground war, Kuwait was liberated by February 28, 1991. About 148 Americans died in combat — far fewer than expected.

fragments.label: q114_fun
fragments.text: After 5 months of buildup, the Persian Gulf War ground assault began February 24, 1991. Just 100 hours later — about 4 days — President Bush declared victory. A 35-nation coalition had pushed Iraq out of Kuwait. The fastest decisive U.S. military victory of its scale in history. But Saddam Hussein stayed in power for 12 more years.

fragments.label: q115_question
fragments.text: What major event happened on September 11, 2001 in the United States?

fragments.label: q115_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q115_answer_1
fragments.text: Terrorists attacked the United States

fragments.label: q115_answer_2
fragments.text: Terrorists took over two planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City

fragments.label: q115_answer_3
fragments.text: Terrorists took over a plane and crashed into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia

fragments.label: q115_answer_4
fragments.text: Terrorists took over a plane originally aimed at Washington, D.C., and crashed in a field in Pennsylvania

fragments.label: q115_why
fragments.text: On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes. Two struck the World Trade Center towers in New York City. One hit the Pentagon. Nearly 3,000 Americans were killed — the deadliest attack on American soil since the Civil War. The country went to war in Afghanistan within weeks. America was changed forever.

fragments.label: q115_fun
fragments.text: On September 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked. The fourth — United Flight 93 — never reached its target. Passengers learned via cell phones what had happened to the other planes, voted to fight back, and stormed the cockpit. The plane crashed in a Shanksville, PA field, 20 minutes from the U.S. Capitol. 40 passengers gave their lives.

fragments.label: q116_question
fragments.text: Name one U.S. military conflict after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

fragments.label: q116_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q116_answer_1
fragments.text: (Global) War on Terror

fragments.label: q116_answer_2
fragments.text: War in Afghanistan

fragments.label: q116_answer_3
fragments.text: War in Iraq

fragments.label: q116_why
fragments.text: After 9/11, the U.S. launched the 'Global War on Terror.' The War in Afghanistan (2001-2021) targeted al-Qaeda and the Taliban government that sheltered them. It became one of America's longest wars along with Vietnam — lasting 20 years. The War in Iraq (2003-2011) overthrew Saddam Hussein but found no weapons of mass destruction. Over 7,000 U.S. troops died in the two wars combined.

fragments.label: q116_fun
fragments.text: On May 1, 2011 — nearly 10 years after 9/11 — Navy SEAL Team Six raided a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan. They killed Osama bin Laden, the al-Qaeda leader who planned the 9/11 attacks. Bin Laden had been hiding in a heavily fortified compound just half a mile from Pakistan's main military academy. President Obama announced it that night.

fragments.label: q117_question
fragments.text: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.

fragments.label: q117_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q117_answer_1
fragments.text: Chippewa

fragments.label: q117_answer_2
fragments.text: Lakota

fragments.label: q117_answer_3
fragments.text: Apache

fragments.label: q117_answer_4
fragments.text: Cherokee

fragments.label: q117_answer_5
fragments.text: Cheyenne

fragments.label: q117_answer_6
fragments.text: Hopi

fragments.label: q117_answer_7
fragments.text: Mohawk

fragments.label: q117_answer_8
fragments.text: Navajo

fragments.label: q117_answer_9
fragments.text: Pueblo

fragments.label: q117_answer_10
fragments.text: Sioux

fragments.label: q117_why
fragments.text: Native Americans have lived on this land for over 15,000 years — long before Europeans arrived. Today there are 574 federally recognized tribes, each a sovereign nation within the United States with its own government. The 25 tribes on the USCIS list span from the Navajo and Pueblo in New Mexico, to the Chippewa and Lakota Minnesota.

fragments.label: q117_fun
fragments.text: In WWII, the U.S. Marines recruited 400+ Navajo soldiers to transmit secret messages in their Navajo language — a code the Japanese NEVER broke. At Iwo Jima, six Code Talkers sent over 800 messages in 48 HOURS, all error-free. A Marine commander said: 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima.'

fragments.label: q118_question
fragments.text: Name one example of an American innovation.

fragments.label: q118_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q118_answer_1
fragments.text: Light bulb

fragments.label: q118_answer_2
fragments.text: Automobile (cars, internal combustion engine)

fragments.label: q118_answer_3
fragments.text: Skyscrapers

fragments.label: q118_answer_4
fragments.text: Airplane

fragments.label: q118_answer_5
fragments.text: Assembly line

fragments.label: q118_answer_6
fragments.text: Landing on the moon

fragments.label: q118_answer_7
fragments.text: Integrated circuit (IC)

fragments.label: q118_why
fragments.text: American innovation transformed daily life worldwide. Edison's light bulb (1879) lit the world. Ford's assembly line (1913) made cars affordable. The Wright Brothers' airplane (1903) shrank the planet. The integrated circuit (1958) powers every phone, computer, and satellite. Landing on the Moon (1969) showed what humans could do.

fragments.label: q118_fun
fragments.text: On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright lay on the lower wing of a homemade airplane at Kitty Hawk, NC, and flew for 12 SECONDS. Distance: 120 feet — shorter than a Boeing 747's wingspan. He and his brother Wilbur were bicycle mechanics from Ohio with no college degrees. Within 66 YEARS of their first flight, a human walked on the Moon.

fragments.label: q119_question
fragments.text: What is the capital of the United States?

fragments.label: q119_answer_1
fragments.text: Washington, D.C.

fragments.label: q119_why
fragments.text: The U.S. capital is Washington, D.C. stands for the District of Columbia. It's not in any state — it's a separate federal district, so no state controls the federal government. Designed in 1791 by French engineer Pierre L'Enfant with diagonal avenues named for states. Home to Congress, the White House, and the Supreme Court.

fragments.label: q119_fun
fragments.text: Before settling in Washington, D.C. in 1800, the U.S. capital moved 8 times. Earlier capitals included Philadelphia, New York City, Princeton New Jersey, Annapolis, Trenton, Baltimore, and York Philadelphia. George Washington, the city's namesake, never lived there. He died in 1799, a year before the capital opened.

fragments.label: q120_question
fragments.text: Where is the Statue of Liberty?

fragments.label: q120_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q120_answer_1
fragments.text: New York (Harbor)

fragments.label: q120_answer_2
fragments.text: Liberty Island

fragments.label: q120_why
fragments.text: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, visible from both New York and New Jersey. For over 130 years, she was the first sight millions of immigrants saw arriving by ship. Emma Lazarus's poem on her pedestal: 'Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.' A universal symbol of freedom.

fragments.label: q120_fun
fragments.text: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France, dedicated October 28, 1886. Sculptor Frédéric Bartholdi designed her. The iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel — yes, the same engineer who built the Eiffel Tower in Paris. She arrived in 350 pieces. Originally shiny copper-colored like a new penny, she turned green from oxidation.

fragments.label: q121_question
fragments.text: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?

fragments.label: q121_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works:

fragments.label: q121_answer_1
fragments.text: (Because there were) 13 original colonies

fragments.label: q121_answer_2
fragments.text: (Because the stripes) represent the original colonies

fragments.label: q121_why
fragments.text: The flag's 13 stripes (7 red, 6 white) represent the original 13 colonies that declared independence from Britain in 1776 and became the first U.S. states from New York down to Georgia along the Atlantic coast. The stripes honor America's founding moment, when 13 separate colonies became one nation.

fragments.label: q121_fun
fragments.text: The first U.S. flag (1777) had 13 stripes AND 13 stars. When Vermont and Kentucky joined, Congress added 2 more of each — the 1795 flag had 15 STRIPES and 15 stars. In 1818, Congress realized they couldn't keep adding stripes forever. They fixed it: 13 stripes PERMANENTLY (for the original colonies), one star per state — forever.

fragments.label: q122_question
fragments.text: Why does the flag have 50 stars?

fragments.label: q122_lead_in
fragments.text: Any one of these works:

fragments.label: q122_answer_1
fragments.text: (Because there is) one star for each state

fragments.label: q122_answer_2
fragments.text: (Because) each star represents a state

fragments.label: q122_answer_3
fragments.text: (Because there are) 50 states

fragments.label: q122_why
fragments.text: The flag's 50 stars represent the 50 states that make up the United States today. Unlike the stripes (fixed at 13 for the original colonies), the stars change every time a new state joins. The current 50-star flag has flown since July 4, 1960 — the year after Hawaii became the 50th state. It is the longest-serving version of the U.S. flag in history.

fragments.label: q122_fun
fragments.text: In 1958, 17-year-old Ohio high schooler Robert Heft designed a 50-star flag as a class project — when there were only 48 states! He predicted Alaska AND Hawaii would join. His teacher gave him a B-. Heft sent it to Washington. President Eisenhower picked his design as the official U.S. flag in 1960. The teacher changed the grade to an A.

fragments.label: q123_question
fragments.text: What is the name of the national anthem?

fragments.label: q123_answer_1
fragments.text: The Star-Spangled Banner

fragments.label: q123_why
fragments.text: 'The Star-Spangled Banner' is sung before sports games, at military ceremonies, and at official events. The words were written by Francis Scott Key in 1814 during the War of 1812, after watching the American flag survive a British attack on Fort McHenry. The original flag he saw is preserved at the Smithsonian.

fragments.label: q123_fun
fragments.text: The melody of 'The Star-Spangled Banner' came from a popular British song! Francis Scott Key wrote the lyrics in 1814 after watching American forces survive a 25-hour British bombardment of Fort McHenry. The tune was 'To Anacreon in Heaven,' a London club song. It didn't become the official national anthem until 1931 — 117 years later.

fragments.label: q124_question
fragments.text: The Nation's first motto was 'E Pluribus Unum.' What does that mean?

fragments.label: q124_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works:

fragments.label: q124_answer_1
fragments.text: Out of many, one

fragments.label: q124_answer_2
fragments.text: We all become one

fragments.label: q124_why
fragments.text: 'E Pluribus Unum' is Latin for 'Out of many, one.' Originally it meant 13 separate colonies becoming one nation. Today it means something even bigger: people from many countries, languages, religions, and backgrounds becoming one American people. It still appears on most U.S. coins and the Great Seal of the United States — the official symbol of our country.

fragments.label: q124_fun
fragments.text: On July 4, 1776 — the same day Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence — they chose Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and Thomas Jefferson to design a national seal. The trio proposed 'E Pluribus Unum.' Look closely: the phrase has exactly 13 letters — one for each original colony.

fragments.label: q125_question
fragments.text: What is Independence Day?

fragments.label: q125_lead_in
fragments.text: Either of these works:

fragments.label: q125_answer_1
fragments.text: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)

fragments.label: q125_answer_2
fragments.text: The country's birthday

fragments.label: q125_why
fragments.text: July 4 (Independence Day, 'the Fourth of July') celebrates the day the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 — formally breaking from Britain. Americans celebrate with fireworks, parades, BBQs, and family gatherings. It became an official federal holiday in 1870. America's 250th birthday is coming up in 2026.

fragments.label: q125_fun
fragments.text: On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted yes for independence. John Adams wrote his wife Abigail: this day will be celebrated forever with 'Pomp and Parade... Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations.' He was right about everything except the date. Congress finalized the Declaration's wording on July 4 — and that's the day America remembered.

fragments.label: term_republic_origin
fragments.text: From the Latin “res publica” — “the public affair.” A republic is a government that belongs to the public, not to a king.

fragments.label: term_republic_def
fragments.text: A country where people pick leaders to make decisions for them — instead of a king deciding everything.

fragments.label: term_republic_word
fragments.text: Republic

fragments.label: term_representative_democracy_def
fragments.text: A government where we vote for people to represent us and make the laws on our behalf.

fragments.label: term_representative_democracy_word
fragments.text: Representative democracy

fragments.label: term_constitution_def
fragments.text: The rulebook for the whole country. It sets up the government and protects people's rights.

fragments.label: term_constitution_word
fragments.text: Constitution

fragments.label: term_popular_sovereignty_origin
fragments.text: A “sovereign” is a supreme ruler, like a king. Sovereignty is the power to rule — so “popular sovereignty” hands that power to the people.

fragments.label: term_popular_sovereignty_def
fragments.text: Sovereignty means the power to rule. Popular sovereignty means that power belongs to the people.

fragments.label: term_popular_sovereignty_word
fragments.text: Popular sovereignty

fragments.label: term_consent_of_the_governed_def
fragments.text: The government only has power because the people agree to give it. “Consent” means to say yes.

fragments.label: term_consent_of_the_governed_word
fragments.text: Consent of the governed

fragments.label: term_social_contract_origin
fragments.text: Think of a contract — an agreement. The “social contract” is the unwritten agreement between people and their government.

fragments.label: term_social_contract_def
fragments.text: An unwritten deal: people agree to follow a government's laws, and in return the government protects them.

fragments.label: term_social_contract_word
fragments.text: Social contract

fragments.label: term_self_government_def
fragments.text: When people rule themselves, instead of being ruled by a king or anyone else.

fragments.label: term_self_government_word
fragments.text: Self-government

fragments.label: term_amendment_origin
fragments.text: Amend means to change — like mending a hole in a dress. (“Mend” even comes from “amend.”)

fragments.label: term_amendment_def
fragments.text: An amendment is an official change or addition to the Constitution.

fragments.label: term_amendment_word
fragments.text: Amendment

fragments.label: term_bill_of_rights_def
fragments.text: The first ten amendments to the Constitution. It lists freedoms the government can't take away.

fragments.label: term_bill_of_rights_word
fragments.text: Bill of Rights
